title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{hao1} (\textbf{Main Theorem}, see~Theorem~\ref{zdlzm}).  Under the above $p$-localization hypothesis, suppose that the cohomology algebra  $H^{*} (C_{f};\mathbb{Z}/p)$ is a trivial algebra, where $C_{f}=S^{n}\cup_{f}e^{n+k+1}\not\simeq*$ with $n\geq2,\,k\geq0$. Then, the homotopy fiber $F$  of  the pinch map  $ \Sigma C_{f}=S^{n+1}\cup _{\Sigma f} e^{n+k+2} \xrightarrow[]{pinch} S^{n+k+2}$ is given by 

\[F=F^{(2)}\cup_{\beta}  e^{3n+2k+3}\cup e^{4n+3k+4}  \cdots,\;\;\big(\beta\in\pi_{3n+2k+2} (F^{(2)})\big).\]  
\noindent
For its attaching map $\beta$,  the following relation holds:
$$\beta \equiv j_{3}  j_{4}\circ \Sigma^{2n+k+2}f\;\mathrm{mod}\, \;I\circ\Sigma^{2n+k+2}f,$$  \noindent for a $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$-submodule  $I\subseteq \pi_{3n+k+2} (F^{(2)})$    whose  precise description is given in Theorem~\ref{zdlzm}.

\upshape(\textbf{The reason for computing   $\pi_{18} (\Sigma^{3}\mathbb{C}P^{2}:2)$}). To compute $\pi_{18} (\Sigma^{3}\mathbb{C}P^{2}:2)$, the essential point is that this group lies in the range where the third cell of the relevant homotopy fiber $F$ matters. Noting that $\Sigma^{3}\mathbb{C}P^{2}\simeq_{p} S^{5}\vee S^{7}$ for each odd prime $p$, the remaining torsions of $\pi_{18} (\Sigma^{3}\mathbb{C}P^{2})$  are straightforwardly determined. title: Remark
body_md:
\upshape(\textbf{The landscape around $\pi_{*} (\Sigma^{3}\mathbb{C}P^{2})$}). The methods in \cite{hp2}  work for
the determination of  
$\pi_{i} (\Sigma^{3}\mathbb{C}P^{2})$ for $i\leq 15$; for $16\leq i\leq 21$, to determine $\pi_{i} (\Sigma^{3}\mathbb{C}P^{2})$, our main  theorem plays a central role. Additionally, our determination of $\pi_{18} (\Sigma^{3}\mathbb{C}P^{2})$ is independent of any information on the groups $\pi_i(\Sigma^{3}\mathbb{C}P^{2})$ with $i\neq18$,  and instead depends only on results for the corresponding homotopy groups of spheres. In fact, to the best of our knowledge, prior to this work there had been no nontrivial determinations of $\pi_{*} (S^{m}\cup e^{r})$ with $r-m\geq 2$ in the $J_{3}$ range. (Here, by a  trivial determination we mean the determination of  a 2-cell complex which is the projective plane $\mathbb{R}P^{2},\;\mathbb{C}P^{2} $ or $\mathbb{H}P^{2}$ or is a wedge sum of spheres. Recall that each homotopy group of $\mathbb{R}P^{2},\;\mathbb{C}P^{2} $ or $\mathbb{H}P^{2}$ is isomorphic to a direct sum of  homotopy groups of spheres.) See Remark \ref{gymt} for the terminology ``in the $J_{3}$ range''. Roughly speaking, this is the range in which the third cell of $F$ affects the computation of $\pi_{*} (\Sigma C_{f})$. All $\pi_{*} (\Sigma C_{f})$ in the $J_{3}$ range are outside the metastable range.

title: Remark
body_md:
\upshape (\textbf{The landscape around $\pi_{*} (S^{n+1}\cup e^{n+k+2})$}). Before the present work, the only known nontrivial determinations of homotopy groups of $2$-cell complexes in the $J_{3}$ range were due to Mukai \cite{xdwp}, Wu \cite{wu2003}, and Zhu-Jin \cite{zzj}. These works all focus on Moore spaces of the form $S^{n}\cup_{2^{i}}e^{n+1}$.


    
 Mukai's approach first determines the attaching map $\beta$ by using James' theorem on relative Whitehead products, and hence does not readily extend to general suspended $2$-cell complexes. Wu's computations avoid an explicit prior determination of $\beta$, but depend  on special decompositions of the loop spaces of mod $2$ Moore spaces, such as Equation~(\ref{pm2fj}). Zhu-Jin again determine $\beta$ by combining Wu's computations, Wu's special splitting of looped$\;\mathrm{mod}\,2$  Moore spaces, and properties of higher Whitehead products. Their method appears to rely substantially on Wu's special ingredients.

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{dlyde} (see Theorem \ref{dlydexj}). Let $p$ be an arbitrary prime, and take homology with coefficients in $\mathbb{Z}/p$. Let  $X=S^{m}\cup e^{r}$, where $2\leq m< r.$ Let $F_{q}$ be the homotopy fiber of the pinch map $q\colon X\rightarrow S^{r}.$ If   $H_{*} (\Omega  X)\cong T(u,v)$ 
as Hopf algebras in which $|u|=m-1,|v|=r-1$,  then  the fiber sequence $\Omega F_{q}\xrightarrow[]{\Omega j} \Omega X \xrightarrow[]{\Omega q}\Omega S^{r}$ induces  a short exact sequence of Hopf algebras
\[H_{*} (\Omega F_{q})\xrightarrow[]{(\Omega j)_{*}} H_{*} (\Omega X) \xrightarrow[]{(\Omega q)_{*}}H_{*} (\Omega S^{r}).\] 
\noindent
Moreover, there exists an isomorphism of Hopf algebras
$$H_{*} (\Omega F_{q})\cong T(\{ \mathrm{ad}^{i} (v)(u)\;|\; i\geq0\} )= T(u,\,[u,v],\,[[u,v],v],\,[[[u,v],v],v],\;\cdots).$$

label: dad
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{dad} (see Theorem \ref{dadxj}).  Let $p$ be  an arbitrary prime, and take homology with coefficients in $\mathbb{Z}/p$. Let $X$ be a finite CW complex with its CW decomposition  $X = X' \cup e^{r}$. Here, $X'\not\simeq *$ is a simply-connected  subcomplex  with $\dim(X')\le r$ and  $\mathrm{rank} (H_{r} (X))=\mathrm{rank} (H_{r} (X'))+1$.\footnote{This equation ensures  that after localization at $p$, there is a classical bijection between  the set of cells of  $X$ and a minimal generating set of $\widetilde{H}_{*} (X)$.  Roughly speaking, it is imposed to avoid cases like  $S^{r-1}\cup_{\mathrm{id}} e^{r}$.}  Let $F_{q}$, $j$ and $q$ be given in the following homotopy fibration, $$F_{q}\stackrel{j}\rightarrow X \xrightarrow[pinch]{q}X/X'=S^{r}.$$  \;\\ \vspace{-2.0\baselineskip}\\
\noindent If $H_{*} (\Omega X)\cong T(\sigma^{-1} (      \widetilde{H}_{*} (X)  ))$ as Hopf algebras,
    then the fiber sequence $\Omega F_{q}\xrightarrow[]{\Omega j} \Omega X \xrightarrow[]{\Omega q}\Omega S^{r}$
 induces  a short exact sequence of Hopf algebras
\[H_{*} (\Omega F_{q})\xrightarrow[]{(\Omega j)_{*}} H_{*} (\Omega X) \xrightarrow[]{(\Omega q)_{*}}H_{*} (\Omega S^{r}).\] 
\noindent In addition, setting \[\sigma^{-1} (      \widetilde{H}_{*} (X))=\mathrm{Span}_{\mathbb{Z}/p}\{  u_{1},u_{2},\cdots,u_{s},v\} \;\text{with}\; |u_{i}|\leq |v| =r-1 \] and $0\neq(\Omega q)_{*} (v)\in H_{r-1} (\Omega S^{r})$, then there exists an isomorphism of Hopf algebras \[H_{*} (\Omega F_{q})\cong T(\{ \mathrm{ad}^{i} (v)(u_{k})\;|\; i\geq0,\; 1\leq k\leq s\} ).\]

title: Remark
body_md:
\upshape(\textbf{Roles of ``Lie brackets'' in homotopy and homology}). In Theorem \ref{dlyde}  and Theorem \ref{dad}, we use  bases of free Lie algebras. It is worth noting that bases of free Lie algebras arise naturally in the Hilton--Milnor splitting. That is, (without taking any localization), for path-connected CW complexes  $X$  and $Y$,
\[
\Omega(\Sigma X \vee \Sigma Y)\;\simeq\; \prod_{w \in B} \, \Omega \Sigma \bigl(X^{\wedge w_x} \wedge Y^{\wedge w_y}\bigr), 
\]
where $B$ is the $\mathbb{Q}$-basis (called the Hall--Lyndon basis) for the free ungraded Lie algebra $L(x,y)$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ such that each element of $B$ is  an iterated Lie bracket  $w$. Each iterated Lie bracket  $w$ is of the form $$[    \cdots   [    [    -,-  ],-   ]  \cdots    ,-   ]$$ with entries $x$ and $y$; 
 (regard $x$ and $y$ as  the  iterated Lie brackets of bracket-length 1).  In the above splitting, $w_x$ and $w_y$ denote the number of $x$'s and $y$'s respectively in the iterated bracket $w$.  The inclusion map from each
factor to the whole looped wedge is given by the loop map of the iterated Whitehead products of the form $$[    \cdots   [    [    -,-  ],-   ]  \cdots    ,-   ]$$ with entries $i\colon\Sigma X \hookrightarrow \Sigma X\vee \Sigma Y$ and $j\colon\Sigma Y \hookrightarrow \Sigma X\vee \Sigma Y$.  See Selick's textbook \cite[Theorem 7.9.4, p.~86]{selickjc}  and Spencer \cite{jj}.

label: neihopf
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{neihopf}  (\textbf{the Bott-Samelson theorem}) Let $X$ be a path-connected space and take homology with
coefficients in a field $\mathbbm{k}$.  Then the following
properties hold. (Recall that by a Hopf algebra $T(V)$ we mean the tensor Hopf algebra  primitively generated by $V$.) 
\begin{itemize}
    \item [\rm (1)]  $H_{*} (\Omega\Sigma X)\cong T(\widetilde{H}_{*} (X))$
    as algebras. (We shall refer to this canonical homomorphism  as the Bott-Samelson homomorphism.)
    \item [\rm (2)]  Let $(T(\widetilde{H}_{*} (X)))'$ be the tensor algebra   $T(\widetilde{H}_{*} (X)).$
    Equip $(T(\widetilde{H}_{*} (X)))'$  with
    a  Hopf algebra structure. Its coproduct  is obtained by extending the homomorphism
     $(\Delta_{X}) _{*}\colon H_{*} (X)\rightarrow H_{*} (X)\otimes H_{*} (X)$, the  coalgebra structure map of $H_{*} (X)$; specifically, the coproduct of $(T(\widetilde{H}_{*} (X)))'$ is determined by the following commutative diagram,
      \[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
 T(\widetilde{H}_{*} (X))\arrow[r] & T(\widetilde{H}_{*} (X))\otimes T(\widetilde{H}_{*} (X)) \\
H_{*} (X) \arrow[r,"(\Delta_{X})_{*}"] \arrow[u,hook] & H_{*} (X)\otimes H_{*} (X). \arrow[u,hook]
\end{tikzcd}
\]   \noindent (This is simply an equivalent description of $(\Delta_{\Omega\Sigma X})_{*}$.)  Then,  $H_{*} (\Omega\Sigma X)\cong (T(\widetilde{H}_{*} (X)))'\;\text{as Hopf algebras}.$ In particular,  $H_{*} (\Omega\Sigma X)\cong T(\widetilde{H}_{*} (X))$ as Hopf algebras if all elements of $\widetilde{H}_{*} (X)$ are primitive.\hfill\boxed{}
\end{itemize}

(Recall the well-known fact that  $(\mathbbm{k}[x])^{*}\cong \Gamma[y]$ as Hopf algebras; disregarding the topological background,  take the  dual of $\frac{\mathbbm{k}[x]}{x^{3}\sim 0}$ as a Hopf algebra and then view the resulting object only as a coalgebra.) Here, $\Gamma[y]$ has its standard $\mathbbm{k}$-basis  $\{  y_{j}\} _{j=0}^{\infty}$ with $|y_{j}|=2j$; by the $n$-stage $\Gamma_{n}[y]$ of $\Gamma[y]$, we mean the $\mathbbm{k}$-vector space spanned by $\{  y_{j}\} _{j=0}^{n}$, equipped with the coproduct obtained by restricting the coproduct of $\Gamma[y]$. Set $u=y_{1},\;v=y_{2}$.  Note that $|u|=2,\;|v|=4$. Then we deduce that $$\Delta_{*} (v)=v\otimes1+1\otimes v+u\otimes u\neq v\otimes1+1\otimes v.$$ 

Since $E\colon \mathbb{C}P^{2}\rightarrow\Omega\Sigma\mathbb{C}P^{2}$ induces a coalgebra monomorphism, we see that $v\in H_{4} (\mathbb{C}P^{2})\subseteq H_{4} (\Omega\Sigma\mathbb{C}P^{2})$ is not primitive in $H_{*} (\Omega\Sigma\mathbb{C}P^{2})$.
        The cases $\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{R}, \mathbb{H}$, and $\mathbb{O}$ can be proved in a similar way.
       \item [\rm (2)] Take $\mathbbm{k}=\mathbb{Z}/3$ and localize spaces at 3. It suffices to note that the homotopy group $\pi_{4} (\emph{S}^{3})=\mathbb{Z}/2\otimes\mathbb{Z}_{(3)}=0$, resulting in $\Sigma \mathbb{C}P^{2}=\emph{S}^{3}\cup e^{5}\simeq\emph{S}^{3}\vee \emph{S}^{5}.$ 

 \item [\rm (3)] We show the case $\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{C}$. Similar proofs
 apply for
$\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{H}\;\text{or}\;\mathbb{O}$.\\
 \indent \quad Now, take $\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{C}.$  Use the notation in the proof of assertion (1).  The homomorphism in assertion (3) of this example is obviously an algebra isomorphism because $T(u,u\otimes u-2v)=T(u,v)$. The element $u\in H_{*} (\Omega\Sigma \mathbb{C}P^{2})$ is clearly primitive. Next we show that $u\otimes u-2v\in H_{*} (\Omega\Sigma\mathbb{C}P^{2})$ is  primitive. The element $\Delta_{*} (u\otimes u-2v)$
 is equal to 
 $$\big(u^{2}\otimes1+1\otimes u^{2}+2u\otimes u\big)-\big(2v\otimes1+1\otimes 2v+2u\otimes u\big)=u^{2}\otimes1+1\otimes u^{2}-2v\otimes1-1\otimes 2v.$$ \noindent  (Here, we denote $u\otimes u\in H_{*} (\Omega\Sigma\mathbb{C}P^{2})$ by $u^{2}$ in order to distinguish internal products from  external products.) body_md:
We need only to prove assertion (1). Assertion (2) and (3) follow from assertion (1) and the property   $$\langle f_{1},f_{2}\rangle=\langle I,I\rangle\circ (f_{1}\wedge f_{2}).$$
\noindent For a topological group $G$, denote by $(-1)$ the $(-1)$-st  power map $G\rightarrow G$, $x\mapsto x^{-1}.$ And denote by $\Delta$ the diagonal map of a space. Now, identify $\Omega\Sigma X$ with a topological group and write $G=\Omega\Sigma X$. Notice that the following composition $\omega$ lifts to $\langle I, I\rangle\colon G\wedge G\rightarrow G$ over the canonical projection, 
    \[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=1.7cm]
\omega\colon G \times G 
\arrow[r, "\Delta \times \Delta"] 
& G^{\times 2} \times G^{\times 2} 
\arrow[r, "(23)"] 
& G^{\times 2} \times G^{\times 2} 
\arrow[r, "{(-1,\,-1) \times(I,\,I)}\;"] 
& G^{\times 2} \times G^{\times 2} 
\arrow[r, "\bar{\mu}"] 
& G.
\end{tikzcd}
\]



\noindent Here, the map $(23)$ is given by $(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4})\mapsto (x_{1},x_{3},x_{2},x_{4})$ and $\bar{\mu}$ is the 4-fold product on $G.$ Suppose that the elements $a,b\in\widetilde{H}_{*} (G)$ are primitive. We examine $\omega_{*} (a\otimes b)$. Clearly, $\Delta_{*} (a)=a\otimes1+1\otimes a$ and $\Delta_{*} (b)=b\otimes1+1\otimes b$.

So, $$(\Delta\times\Delta)_{*} (a\otimes b)=(a\otimes1+1\otimes a)\otimes(b\otimes1+1\otimes b)=a\otimes 1\otimes b\otimes 1+a\otimes 1\otimes 1\otimes b+1\otimes a\otimes b\otimes 1+1\otimes a\otimes 1\otimes b.$$ \noindent
Then, $(23)_{*} (\Delta\times\Delta)_{*} (a\otimes b)$ is  equal to $$a\otimes b\otimes 1\otimes 1+a\otimes 1\otimes 1\otimes b+(-1)^{|a||b|}1\otimes b\otimes a\otimes 1+1\otimes 1\otimes a\otimes b. $$
\noindent Note that $(-1)_{*} (1)=1$,  $(-1)_{*} (a)=-a$ and $(-1)_{*} (b)=-b$.  It follows that $((-1,-1)\times (I,I))_{*} (\Delta\times\Delta)_{*} (a\otimes b)$
is $$a\otimes b\otimes 1\otimes 1-a\otimes 1\otimes 1\otimes b-(-1)^{|a||b|}1\otimes b\otimes a\otimes 1+1\otimes 1\otimes a\otimes b .$$ Hence, $\omega_{*} (a\otimes b)=\bar{\mu}_{*} ((-1,-1)\times (I,I))_{*} (\Delta\times\Delta)_{*} (a\otimes b)=[a,b].$ Therefore, $\langle I, I\rangle_{*} (a\otimes b)=[a,b].$

\label{grdl} (\cite{Gray,hp2}) Let $X$ be a path-connected  \textit{CW}  complex and $A$ be its path-connected  subcomplex. Let $i\colon  A\hookrightarrow X$  be the inclusion. Then we have the inclusion  $i\colon  (A,A)\hookrightarrow (X,A)$.
The following statements hold.
\begin{itemize}

\item[\rm(1)]\label{grdl1a} $J(A,A)=J(A)$, where $J(A)$ is the ordinary James construction. There exists a fiber sequence\vspace{-0.6\baselineskip}
\[\begin{tikzcd}
   J(A) 
    \arrow[r,hook, "J(i)"] 
  & J(X,A) 
    \arrow[r] 
  & X \cup_{i} CA 
    \arrow[r, "p"] 
  & \Sigma A,
\end{tikzcd}\]  
\noindent where $p$ is  the pinch map, $ J(i)$ is the inclusion   extended over   $i\colon  (A,A)\hookrightarrow (X,A)$.  Moreover, if  $$K\stackrel{g}\longrightarrow L \stackrel{j_{_{L}}} \longrightarrow C_{g}\stackrel{q}\longrightarrow\Sigma K$$ \noindent is a cofiber sequence where  $K$,\;$L$ are path-connected  \textit{CW}  complexes,\; then there exists a fiber sequence \;\vspace{-0.6\baselineskip} 
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=0.8cm]
   J(K) \arrow[r,hook,"J(i_g)"] & J(M_L, K) \arrow[r] & C_g \arrow[r, "q"] & \Sigma K,
\end{tikzcd}\]
\noindent where \textbf{$M_{L}$ is the mapping cylinder of $g$}, and 
$ J(i_{g})$  is the inclusion   extended over  $i_{g} \colon  (K,K)\hookrightarrow (M_{L}, K)$.
\item[\rm(2)]\label{grdl2a}   If  $X/A$ is path-connected, and  $\Omega\Sigma A$,  $X/A$ are \textit{CW} complexes of finite type,  (for example, $X$ is a finite simply-connected CW complex and $A$ is its skeleton), then$$\widetilde{H}_{\ast} (J(X,A); \mathbbm{k})\cong \widetilde{H}_{\ast} (X;\mathbbm{k})\otimes H_{\ast} (\Omega\Sigma A;\mathbbm{k})\;\;\text{ where} \;\mathbbm{k}\;\text{is a field}.$$

label: gymt
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{gymt} \begin{itemize}
    \item[\rm (1)]  Let $X=S^{n+1}\cup e^{n+k+2}\not\simeq*$  ($n\geq1$ and $k\geq0$) be a space which is not required to be a suspension. 
If $i \ge 3n+2k+2$, we say that the groups $\pi_i(X)$ lie in the range in which the third cell of the homotopy fiber contributes; or, more briefly, that they lie in the $J_{3}$ range. 
This terminology is justified as follows. Applying Gray's result (Proposition \ref{grdl}), the homotopy fiber  of 
$X \xrightarrow[]{pinch} S^{n+k+1}$ admits a CW decomposition  
$$
J(M_{S^{n+1}},S^{n+k+1}) = S^{n+1} \cup e^{2n+k+2} \cup e^{3n+2k+3} \cup e^{4n+3k+4}\cup\cdots,
$$\noindent
(similar to Equation (\ref{jhaaa}) explained in the above remark). The third cell \[e^{3n+2k+3} \subseteq J_{3} (M_{S^{n+1}}, S^{n+k+1})\subseteq J(M_{S^{n+1}}, S^{n+k+1})\] contributes the groups $\pi_i(X)$ with $i \ge 3n+2k+2$.
\item[\rm (2)] Let $X$ be an $((n+1)-1)$-connected space with $\pi_{n+1} (X)\neq0$. Usually, the groups $\pi_{i} (X)$ with $2n+1\leq i\leq 3n+1$ (sometimes just with $i\leq 3n+1$)  are said to be in the metastable range. In this range, the generalized $EHP$ sequence applies and the canonical map $X\hookrightarrow J(X)$ can be identified with its restriction $X\hookrightarrow J_{2} (X)$. See the standard materials such as Hatcher \cite[p.~474]{xh} and Whitehead \cite[Theorem 2.2, p.~548]{GW}.
\item[\rm (3)]Use the notation in assertion (1). In general, for  groups $\pi_{*} (X)$, the condition of being in the $J_{3}$ range is strictly stronger than that of being outside the metastable range. Each group $\pi_i(X)$  in the $J_{3}$ range is outside  the metastable range. 
Conversely, if  $\pi_i(X)$ is  unstable and  outside  the metastable range, i.e., $i\geq 3n+2$, then $\pi_i(X)$ may not be in the $J_{3}$ range. Note  that $[3n+2k+2,\infty]\subsetneq [3n+2,\infty]$ when $k\geq1$.\end{itemize}

body_md:
\label{zzd} Localize spaces at  a prime $p$. Let
\[
S^{m}\stackrel{g}\longrightarrow Y\stackrel{i}\hookrightarrow X = Y\cup_{g} e^{m+1}
\]
be a  cofiber sequence, where $Y$ is a simply-connected CW complex of finite type with $\dim(Y)\le m$; if $\mathrm{dim} (Y)=m$, additionally assume that the homomorphism $g_{*}=H_{m} (g)$ is trivial.
 Denote the homotopy fiber of $Y\stackrel{i}\hookrightarrow X$ by $F_{i}$. Let $S^{m}=\mathrm{sk}_{m} (F_{i})\stackrel{\,j'}\hookrightarrow F_{i}$ and $F_{i}\stackrel{j}\rightarrow Y$ be the  skeleton inclusion and  the homotopy fiber inclusion, respectively. Then  $ g= jj'\in\pi_{m} (Y)$
up to a unit in  $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$.

title: Proof
body_md:
By observing the $\mathbb{Z}/p$-homology Leray-Serre spectral sequence associated with the homotopy fibration $F_{i}\rightarrow Y\rightarrow X$, we infer $\mathrm{sk}_{m} (F_{i})=S^{m}.$ Consider the exact sequence $\pi_{m} (F_{i})\stackrel{j_{*}}\longrightarrow \pi_{m} (Y)\stackrel{i_{*}}\longrightarrow \pi_{m} (Y\cup_{g} e^{m+1})$, that is, the exact sequence 
$\langle \,j'\,\rangle\stackrel{j_{*}}\longrightarrow \pi_{m} (Y)\rightarrow \pi_{m} (Y)/\langle g\rangle$.  (Here, we make free use of the fundamental techniques for computing homotopy groups; see Remark~\ref{jssq} for an account of these techniques.) The exactness forces  $\langle\, j_{*} (j')\,\rangle=\langle g\rangle$. Hence the result holds.

body_md:
\label{sfrc}
Localize spaces at  a prime $p$. Let $X$ be a simply-connected CW complex of finite type and write  $H_{m} (S^{m})=\langle \iota\rangle$. Suppose that there exists a map  $g\in\pi_{m} (X)$  with $m\geq2$ such that  $0\neq g_{*} (\iota)\in H_{m} (X)$. (Such an element $g_{*} (\iota)$, a$\;\mathrm{mod}\, p$ Hurewicz image,  is said to be$\;\mathrm{mod}\, p$ spherical.)  Then the following assertions hold.
\begin{itemize}
    \item[\rm(1)] $\mathrm{sk}_{m} (X)\simeq K\vee S^{m}$ for some simply-connected  CW complex $K$  with  $\mathrm{dim} (K)\leq m$. 
     \item[\rm(2)] The$\;\mathrm{mod}\, p$ spherical splitting is natural.  Namely, let $h\colon X\rightarrow Y$ be a map where $Y$ is a simply-connected CW complex of finite type. If  $0\neq h_{*}g_{*} (\iota)$ in $ H_{m} (Y)$, then, up to a unit in $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$, there exists a commutative diagram  in which $h_{m}$ denotes the restriction of $h$, \vspace{-1.5\baselineskip}\;\\ \[\begin{tikzcd}
		S^m 
		\arrow[r,hook]
		\arrow[d, equal]
		\arrow[rrr, bend left=20, "g"] 
		& K \vee S^m \arrow[d]
		\arrow[r, "\simeq"]
		& \mathrm{sk}_m X 
		\arrow[r, hookrightarrow]             
		\arrow[d, "h_{m}"]
		& X
		\arrow[d, "h"]
		\\
		S^m
		\arrow[r,hook]
		\arrow[rrr, bend right=20, " h\circ g "]
		& K' \vee S^m
		\arrow[r, "\simeq"]
		& \mathrm{sk}_m Y
		\arrow[r, hook]             
		& Y.
	\end{tikzcd}
	\]

\end{itemize}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The result is standard, so we give a streamlined proof.
\begin{itemize}
    \item [\rm (1)]Let the map $g_{m}\colon  S^{m}\rightarrow\mathrm{sk}_{m} (X) $ be the restriction of $g$. It is sufficient to  assume that there exists a cell $e^{m}\subseteq X$ such that the composition $$q\circ g_{m}\colon   S^{m}\stackrel{g_{m}}\longrightarrow\mathrm{sk}_{m} (X) \xrightarrow[proj.]{q}\frac{\mathrm{sk}_{m} (X)}{\mathrm{sk}_{m} (X)\backslash e^{m}}=S^{m}$$
induces an isomorphism of the $m$-th$\;\mathrm{mod}\, p$ homology groups. (If $X$ has multiple $m$-cells, such a desired cell $e^{m}$ may not exist; nevertheless, by using some self homotopy equivalence in $[\bigvee _{finite}S^{m-1},\bigvee _{finite}S^{m-1}]$, we see that there exists a CW complex $M$  such that $M\simeq\mathrm{sk}_{m} (X)$ and $M$ has  such a desired cell $e^{m}$.  If $X$ has only one $m$-cell $e^{m}$, the desired property of $e^{m}$ holds automatically.) Then,  we obtain $q\circ g_{m}=\mathrm{id}_{S^{m}}$ up to a unit in $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$.
Choose $K$ as $\mathrm{sk}_{m} (X)\backslash e^{m}$. Consequently, we have a cofiber sequence for some attaching map $\mathrm{a}$, \[ S^{m-1}\stackrel{\mathrm{a}}\longrightarrow K\rightarrow\mathrm{sk}_{m} (X)\stackrel{q}\longrightarrow S^{m}.\] Applying the Blakers--Massey theorem or Gray's relative James construction (Proposition \ref{grdl}), we deduce an exact sequence 
 \[ \pi_{m} (\mathrm{sk}_{m} (X))\stackrel{q_{*}\,}\longrightarrow \pi_{m} (S^{m})\stackrel{\partial}\rightarrow \pi_{m-1} (K).\]
Since $q_{*}=\pi_{m} (q)$ is surjective, we have     $\partial(\mathrm{id_{S^{m}}})=\mathrm{a}=0$.\item [(\rm 2)] Similar to the proof of assertion (1), it is sufficient to  assume that  $Y$ has a  cell $e^{m}$ corresponding to the generator $(hg)_{*} (\iota)\in H_{m} (Y)$.  Take $K'$ as the CW complex $\mathrm{sk}_{m} (Y)\backslash e^{m}$. The remaining parts  can be checked by a standard diagram chase. The situation is analogous to that in the category of  abelian groups.
\end{itemize}

body_md:
\label{tl}Localize  spaces at  a prime $p$. Let $X=S^{m}\cup _{h}e^{r} \not\simeq*$ be given where $1\leq m<r$. Set the homology
$\widetilde{H}_*(X)=\mathrm{Span}_{\mathbb{Z}/p}\{  u,v\} $ where    $|u| = m$ and  $|v| = r$. Denote by $\iota_{m+r}$ the generator of $ H_{m+r} (S^{m+r})\cong\mathbb{Z}/p.$
 \begin{itemize} 

\item [\rm(1)] If $p=2$,  then there exists a map $g \colon S^{m+r} \longrightarrow X \wedge X$ such that $$0\neq g_{*} (\iota_{m+r})=uv-vu=[u,v]\in H_{m+r} (X \wedge X  )).$$
 \item [\rm (2)] If $p\geq3$, then there exists a map $g \colon S^{m+r} \longrightarrow X \wedge X$ and some integer $t\in [1,p-1]$
 such that $$0\neq g_{*} (\iota_{m+r})=uv+tvu\in H_{m+r} (X \wedge X  )).$$

\end{itemize}

label: cfb1
title: Proof
body_md:
Consider the homotopy cofibration $X\wedge S^{r-1} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{id}_X\wedge h} X\wedge S^m\xrightarrow{\mathrm{id}_X\wedge i} X\wedge X$  where       $i\colon S^{n}\rightarrow X$ denotes the inclusion of the bottom cell.
\noindent Take the $(2r-1)$--skeleton of $X\wedge X$ and note that $S^m\wedge S^{r-1} \simeq \mathrm{sk}_{2r-2} (X\wedge S^{r-1})$;
hence we obtain a homotopy cofibration \begin{equation}\label{cfb1}
    S^m\wedge S^{r-1} \xrightarrow{i\wedge h} X\wedge S^m
\to \mathrm{sk}_{2r-1} (X\wedge X).
\end{equation}
\noindent  Next we will show that $i\wedge h=*$. Since $i\wedge h$
is equal to the composition
\[
S^m\wedge S^{r-1}
\xrightarrow{\mathrm{id}_{S^m}\wedge h}
S^m\wedge S^m
\xrightarrow{i\wedge \mathrm{id}_{S^m}}
X\wedge S^m,
\]
we obtain the  commutative diagram the with the bottom row a homotopy cofibration
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large,row sep=large]
S^{m}\wedge S^{r-1}
\arrow[r,"\mathrm{id}_{S^{m}}\wedge h"]
\arrow[d,"\tau'"']
&
S^{m}\wedge S^{m}
\arrow[d,"\tau"]
\\
S^{r-1}\wedge S^{m}
\arrow[r,"h\wedge \mathrm{id}_{S^{m}}"]
&
S^{m}\wedge S^{m}
\arrow[r,"i\wedge \mathrm{id}_{S^{m}}"]
&
X\wedge S^{m},
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\noindent   
where  $\tau'$ and $\tau$ are the switching maps.   So, $$(i\wedge \mathrm{id}_{S^{m}})\circ[\pm 1]\circ(\mathrm{id}_{S^{m}}\wedge h)=(i\wedge \mathrm{id}_{S^{m}})\circ(h\wedge \mathrm{id}_{S^{m}})\circ[\pm 1]=*.$$
\noindent The left side of this equation is just $\pm(i\wedge h)$.
Thus, $i\wedge h=*$ in the homotopy cofibration (\ref{cfb1}). Therefore $$\mathrm{sk}_{2r-1} (X\wedge X)\simeq (\Sigma ^{m}X)\vee S^{m+r}.$$
\noindent   
Define $g'$ to be the composition of the  inclusions $S^{m+r}\stackrel{i_{0}}\hookrightarrow \mathrm{sk}_{2r-1} (X\wedge X)
\hookrightarrow X\wedge X.$ Then  $0\neq g'_{*} (\iota_{m+r})$ is$\;\mathrm{mod}\, p$ spherical. 

Consider  the case $p=2$. If $\Sigma^{m}X\not\simeq S^{2m}\vee S^{m+r}$, then neither $uv$ nor $vu$ is$\;\mathrm{mod}\,2$ spherical in $$H_{m+r} (X\wedge X )=\{ 0,uv,uv,[u,v]\} ,$$ which forces
$[u,v]$ to be$\;\mathrm{mod}\,2$ spherical. Thus $g'_{*} (\iota_{m+r})=[u,v]$. In this case, take $g=g'.$ If $\Sigma^{m}X\simeq S^{2m}\vee S^{m+r}$, then all elements in $H_{m+r} (X\wedge X )$  are$\;\mathrm{mod}\,2$ spherical; note that we can make use of the self homotopy equivalences in $[S^{m+r}\vee S^{m+r},S^{m+r}\vee S^{m+r}]$ to change the basis of $H_{m+r} (\mathrm{sk}_{2r-1} (X\wedge X))$. In this case, take $g$ to be the composition $$S^{m+r}\stackrel{i_{0}}\hookrightarrow
\mathrm{sk}_{2r-1} (X\wedge X)\xrightarrow[\simeq]{e} \mathrm{sk}_{2r-1} (X\wedge X)
\hookrightarrow X\wedge X$$
for some self homotopy equivalence $e$ in $[\mathrm{sk}_{2r-1} (X\wedge X),\mathrm{sk}_{2r-1} (X\wedge X)]\cong[S^{2m}\vee S^{m+r}\vee S^{m+r},S^{2m}\vee S^{m+r}\vee S^{m+r}].$

Consider  the case $p\geq3$.  If $\Sigma^{m}X\not\simeq S^{2m}\vee S^{m+r}$, then  neither $uv$ nor $vu$ is$\;\mathrm{mod}\, p$ spherical in $$H_{m+r} (X\wedge X )=\{  xuv,yuv\;|\;0\leq x\leq p-1,\;0\leq y\leq p-1\} ,$$ which forces $g_{*} (\iota_{m+r})=t_{1}uv+t_{2}vu$  for some integers $t_{1},t_{2}\in [1,p-1].$  Then choose $g=\frac{1}{t_{1}}g'$, satisfying the desired property. If $\Sigma^{m}X\simeq S^{2m}\vee S^{m+r}$, then all elements in $H_{m+r} (X\wedge X )$  are$\;\mathrm{mod}\, p$ spherical; similar to  the case $p=2$, we can find the desired map $g$ by using the  self homotopy equivalence.

label: dlydexj
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{dlydexj}  Let  $X=S^{m}\cup e^{r}$ be given where $2\leq m< r.$ Let $F_{q}$ be the homotopy fiber of the pinch map $q\colon  X\rightarrow S^{r}.$ If   $H_{*} (\Omega  X)\cong T(u,v)$ 
as Hopf algebras in which $|u|=m-1,|v|=r-1$,  then  the fiber sequence $\Omega F_{q}\xrightarrow[]{\Omega j} \Omega X \xrightarrow[]{\Omega q}\Omega S^{r}$ induces  a short exact sequence of Hopf algebras
\[H_{*} (\Omega F_{q})\xrightarrow[]{(\Omega j)_{*}} H_{*} (\Omega X) \xrightarrow[]{(\Omega q)_{*}}H_{*} (\Omega S^{r}).\] 
\noindent
Moreover, there exists an isomorphism of Hopf algebras
$$H_{*} (\Omega F_{q})\cong T(\{ \mathrm{ad}^{i} (v)(u)\;|\; i\geq0\} )= T(u,\,[u,v],\,[[u,v],v],\,[[[u,v],v],v],\;\cdots).$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
In fact, this theorem is essentially due to Cohen-Moore-Neisendorfer \cite[Proposition~9.3, Corollary~9.4]{CMN1979}. The goal of our proof is to verify that their method (which is outlined quite briefly, with numerous steps  omitted) remains effective in the context of the  generalized hypotheses. The verifications are divided into 4 steps.  Set the homology $H_{*} (\Omega S^{r} )=T(\iota)$ where $|\iota|=r-1$.\;\vspace{-0.5\baselineskip}\;\\\\
\noindent\textbf{STEP-1} Examine the $(\Omega q)_{*}$-images.  We show that $(\Omega q)_{*} (u)=0$ and  $(\Omega q)_{*} (v)=\iota$  up to a unit in $\mathbb{Z}/p$;  hence we may reset the homology $H_{*} (\Omega S^{r} )=T(\iota)$ with $|\iota|=r-1$   and  $(\Omega q)_{*} (v)=\iota.$ 

First we analyze $(\Omega q)_{*} (v)$. Consider the $\mathbb{Z}/p$-homology Leray-Serre spectral sequence $\{  E^{\bullet}_{\bullet,\bullet},d_{\bullet}\} $ associated with the homotopy fibration $\Omega X\rightarrow*\rightarrow X$. By  Proposition \ref{mdpxl}, this  spectral sequence is a  $H_{*} (\Omega X)$-module spectral sequence, $d(ab)=(da)b$. Set $\widetilde{H}_{*} (X)=\mathrm{Span}_{\mathbb{Z}/p}\{  u', v'\} $ with $|u'|=m,\,|v'|=r$ and $d_{m} (u')=u$. In the $E^{m}$-page, $d(u')=u$, $d(u'\alpha)= (du')\alpha= u\alpha$ for each $\alpha\in E^{m}_{0,\bullet}$. Note that in $E^{m}_{0,\bullet}\cong E^{2}_{0,\bullet}$, $v\neq u\alpha$ for each  $\alpha\in E^{m}_{0,\bullet}$. So $v\in E^{2}_{0,r-1}$ survives to $E^{2m}_{0,r-1}.$ Then we infer that  $d(v')=\ell v$ for some $1\leq\ell\leq p-1$. Notice that there is an obvious momorphism from the homtopy fibration $\Omega X\rightarrow*\rightarrow X$ to the homtopy fibration $\Omega S^{r}\rightarrow*\rightarrow S^{r}$ induced by the map $q$.
Thus,
 $(\Omega q)_{*} (v)=\ell\iota$,  
resulting from the  naturality of the transgressions of the Leray-Serre spectral sequences. By this naturality, we also obtain $(\Omega q)_{*} (u)=0$.
\;\vspace{-0.5\baselineskip}\\

\noindent\textbf{STEP-2} We proceed to justify that the comodule $H_{*} (\Omega X )$ is an injective right $H_{*} (\Omega S^{r} )$-comodule.  Write tensors $a\otimes b$ in $T(u,v)$ as $ab$ rather than $a\otimes b$.  At the purely algebraic level, we may use the identification of Hopf algebras $$H_{*} (\Omega S^{r} )=T(v)\subseteq T(u,v).$$ Additionally,  $H_{*} (\Omega X )=T(u,v)$ is a right $H_{*} (\Omega S^{r} )$-module whose module structure map is given by $$T(u,v)\otimes T(v)\rightarrow T(u,v),\;a\otimes b\mapsto ab.$$ \noindent That is, $a\star b=ab$. Meanwhile, $H_{*} (\Omega X) $ is a right $H_{*} (\Omega S^{r})$-comodule  with its canonical  comodule structure map $$\rho_{*}\colon  H_{*} (\Omega X )\rightarrow H_{*} (\Omega X)\otimes H_{*} (\Omega S^{r} ),\;\text{where}\; \rho=(\Omega\mathrm{id},\Omega q)\colon \Omega X\rightarrow \Omega X\times \Omega S^{r}.$$ Observe that $\rho=(\Omega\mathrm{id},*)\cdot (*,\Omega q)$, the product of maps resulting from the $H$-structure. So,  $$\rho_{*} (u)=u\otimes1, \;\;\rho_{*} (v)=v\otimes1+1\otimes v=\Delta_{*} (v),$$ \noindent where $\Delta\colon \Omega S^{r}\rightarrow \Omega S^{r}\times \Omega S^{r}$ denotes the diagonal map. We know that $\rho_{*}$ and $\Delta_{*}$ are algebra homomorphisms since $\rho$ and $\Delta$ can be identified with the loop maps. Let $i\geq1$. We have $$\rho_{*} (v^{i})=(\rho_{*} (v))^{i}=(\Delta_{*} (v))^{i}=\Delta_{*} (v^{i})=\sum (v^{i})_{1}\otimes (v^{i})_{2}.$$
\noindent
Take an arbitrary $\beta\in T(u,v)=H_{*} (\Omega X )$. Then, $\rho_{*} (\beta)=\sum \beta_{(0)}\otimes\beta_{(1)}$. Hence, $\rho_{*} (\beta\star v^{i})$ is equal to $$\rho_{*} (\beta v^{i})=\rho_{*} (\beta)\rho_{*} ( v^{i})=(\sum \beta_{(0)}\otimes\beta_{(1)})(\sum (v^{i})_{1}\otimes (v^{i})_{2})=\sum (\beta_{(0)} (v^{i})_{1})\otimes(\beta_{(1)} (v^{i})_{2})=\sum (\beta_{(0)}\star(v^{i})_{1})\otimes(\beta_{(1)} (v^{i})_{2}).$$

\noindent So, $H_{*} (\Omega X )$ is a  right $H_{*} (\Omega S^{r} )$-Hopf module. Then, by Proposition \ref{emsdy}, we see that $$H_{*} (\Omega X )\cong (H_{*} (\Omega X ))^{\mathrm{co}\,H_{*} (\Omega S^{r} )} \otimes H_{*} (\Omega S^{r} )$$ 
\noindent as right $H_{*} (\Omega S^{r} )$-Hopf modules. It follows that  $H_{*} (\Omega X )$ is   a free  right $H_{*} (\Omega S^{r} )$-comodule, therefore an injective  right $H_{*} (\Omega S^{r} )$-comodule. (Recall that a right $C$-comodule $M$ is said to be free if $M\cong N\otimes C$ as right $C$-comodules for some vector space $N$.)\\ \vspace{-0.6\baselineskip}\\
\noindent\textbf{STEP-3} Use the Eilenberg-Moore  spectral sequence.


Applying  \cite[Theorem~3.2]{ms1} and \cite[Proposition~3.1]{ms1}  for the homotopy pull-back of $\Omega X\rightarrow\Omega S^{r} \leftarrow *$,   we have a  spectral sequence $\{  E^{\bullet}_{\bullet,\bullet},d_{\bullet}\} \Rightarrow H_{*} (\Omega F_{q})$ with $$E^{2}\cong\mathrm{Cotor}^{H_{*} (\Omega S^{r})} ( H_{*} (\Omega X),\mathbb{Z}/p)\text{\,\;as differential (graded) Hopf algebras}.$$ 
The deleted injective resolution of $H_{*} (\Omega X)$ contains a unique  nonzero item, $H_{*} (\Omega X)$. Then the  differential graded Hopf algebra $\mathrm{Cotor}^{H_{*} ( \Omega S^{r})} ( H_{*} (\Omega X),\mathbb{Z}/p)$  has only trivial differentials and hence the spectral sequence collapses at $E^{2}$-page. Combining  with STEP 2 and the definition of the functor 
$\mathrm{Cotor}$,  we have  $$H_{*} (\Omega 
 F_{q})\cong H_{*} (\Omega X)\boxed{}_{H_{*} (\Omega S^{r})}\mathbb{Z}/p= T(u,v)\boxed{}_{T(\iota)}\mathbb{Z}/p\text{\; as  Hopf algebras.}$$
 

\noindent\textbf{STEP-4}  We justify that 
$T(u,v)\,\boxed{}_{ T(\iota)} \mathbb{Z}/p=T(\{ \mathrm{ad}^{i} (v)(u)\;|\; i\geq0\} ).$  (Here, we use ``='' since $T(u,v)\,\boxed{}_{ T(\iota)} \mathbb{Z}/p$ is canonically viewed as as a subset of $T(u,v).$)



In order to complete this step, we need
   carry out a calculation of the Euler-Poincar\'e series, parallel to the calculation in the proof of \cite[Proposition~4.5, p.~135]{CMN1979}. (Regrettably, the symbols $V$ and $W$  are used with quite different meanings in \cite[Lemma~3.13, p.~132]{CMN1979} and \cite[Corollary 3.11, p.~131]{CMN1979}, which may cause confusion. Here, we follow the convention of \cite[Lemma~3.13, p.~132]{CMN1979}.)




Let $L(-)$ be the free Lie algebra functor. Consider the  epimorphism $L(u, v)\rightarrow L(v)$ given by $u\mapsto0,\; v\mapsto v$. Let $L_{0}=L(V')$   be the kernel of this epimorphism. (Note that this kernel is freely generated; this follows from  
\cite[Corollary~3.11, p.~132]{CMN1979}.) Then we have a short exact sequence of free Lie algebras \vspace{-0.5\baselineskip}
\[\begin{tikzcd}
L_0 \arrow[r] 
    \arrow[d, equals] 
  & L \arrow[r] 
      \arrow[d, equals] 
  & L'' 
      \arrow[d, equals] \\L(V')  
  & L(u, v)  
  & L(v).
\end{tikzcd}\]
\noindent Applying the universal enveloping algebra functor $U(-)$, we have a short exact sequence of Hopf algebras,
\[\begin{tikzcd}
A' \arrow[r] 
    \arrow[d, equals] 
  & A \arrow[r] 
      \arrow[d, equals] 
  & A'' 
      \arrow[d, equals] \\UL(V')  
  & UL(u, v)  
  & UL(v).
\end{tikzcd}\]
\noindent We calculate the  Euler-Poincar\'e series of $V'$ following \cite[Corollary 3.11, p.~132]{CMN1979}, $$\chi (V)=1-(\sum_{i=0}^{\infty} (t^{r-1})^{i})\cdot(1-t^{m-1}-t^{r-1})=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\,t^{m-1+i(r-1)}.$$
\noindent Note that the Hopf algebra $T(V')=UL(V')$. By \cite[Lemma~3.12, Lemma~3.13, p.~132]{CMN1979}, we see that the module  of indecomposable elements  $$Q(A')=Q(UL(V'))=Q(T(V'))=V'$$ becomes a free 
$T(v)$-module  with $v$ acting on $V'$ by 
$\mathrm{ad}^{i} (v)(-)$.  Thus,   $V'$ has $\mathrm{ad}^{i} (v)(u)\; ( i\geq0)$ as a $\mathbb{Z}/p$-basis. Then, by the definition of short exact sequences of Hopf algebras (\cite[Definition 3.3, p.~129]{CMN1979}),  we obtain  $$T(u,v)\,\boxed{}_{ T(\iota)} \mathbb{Z}/p=UL(V'),$$ \noindent completing the proof.

title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{gylpj} Follow the notation in Theorem \ref{dlydexj} and use the identification $H_{*} (\Omega F_{q})= T(\{ \mathrm{ad}^{i} (v)(u)\;|\; i\geq0\} ).$ Let $j\colon   F_{q}\rightarrow X$ be the inclusion of the homotopy fiber in the homotopy fibration $F_{q}\stackrel{j}\rightarrow X \xrightarrow[pinch]{q}S^{r}.$
    Then,  for each $\mathrm{ad}^{i} (v)(u)\in H_{*} (\Omega F_{q})$, we have $(\Omega j)_{*} (\mathrm{ad}^{i} (v)(u))=\mathrm{ad}^{i} (v)(u)\in  H_{*} (\Omega X).$ \hfill \boxed{}

label: jsxs
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{jsxs} In  Cohen-Moore-Neisendorfer  \cite[p.~149]{CMN1979}, they consider the ground ring ``$R=\mathbb{Z}/p^{s}\mathbb{Z}$ with  $1\leq s \leq r$ if $p$ is an odd prime and with $s = 1$ if $p = 2$''.  In their \cite[Corollary~9.4, p.~150]{CMN1979}, the ground ring is taken as such a ring $R$. In  Theorem \ref{dlyde} (Theorem \ref{dlydexj}),
the integral  homology groups of the spaces $C_{f}$, $F$ and $\Omega F$ are torsion free if $m-r\geq2$.
Replacing   the ground ring $\mathbb{Z}/p$ in  Theorem \ref{dlyde} (Theorem \ref{dlydexj})  by  the above ring $R$ has no influence on the proof and  the theorem remains true.   For the study of $p$-local simply connected CW complexes of finite type, homology with $\mathbb{Z}/p$ coefficients is the primary object of interest.

title: Proof
body_md:
This theorem is still essentially due to Cohen-Moore-Neisendorfer \cite[Proposition~9.3, Corollary~9.4]{CMN1979}. Their methods apply in this more general case.

Note that the setting $0\neq(\Omega q)_{*} (v)\in H_{r-1} (\Omega S^{r})$ is reasonable, by the method of the proof of Theorem \ref{dlydexj}.
To prove  Sequence (\ref{zhl}) is exact, the methods of the proofs of Theorem \ref{dlydexj} and Corollary \ref{gylpj} remain workable in this more general case.   We only show the isomorphism given in Equation (\ref{adivuk}) in view of the last step of the proof of Theorem \ref{dlydexj}.

Recall that $L(-)$ is the free Lie algebra functor. Let $|u_{k}|=m_{k}$. Consider the  epimorphism $L(\{  u_{k}\} , v)\rightarrow L(v)$ given by $u_{k}\mapsto0,\; v\mapsto v$. Let $L_{0}=L(V')$   be the kernel of this epimorphism.  Then we have a short exact sequence of free Lie algebras \vspace{-0.8\baselineskip}
\[\begin{tikzcd}
L_0 \arrow[r] 
    \arrow[d, equals] 
  & L \arrow[r] 
      \arrow[d, equals] 
  & L'' 
      \arrow[d, equals] \\L(V')  
  & L(\{  u_{k}\} , v)  
  & L(v).
\end{tikzcd}\]
\noindent Applying the universal enveloping algebra functor $U(-)$, we have a short exact sequence of Hopf algebras,
\[\begin{tikzcd}
A' \arrow[r] 
    \arrow[d, equals] 
  & A \arrow[r] 
      \arrow[d, equals] 
  & A'' 
      \arrow[d, equals] \\UL(V')  
  & UL(\{  u_{k}\} , v)  
  & UL(v).
\end{tikzcd}\]
\noindent Note that $H_{*} (\Omega F_{q})=UL(V')$. We calculate the  Euler-Poincar\'e series of $V'$ according to \cite[Corollary 3.11, p.~132]{CMN1979}, \begin{align}
\chi(V') &= \notag 1-(\sum_{h=0}^{\infty}\,(t^{r-1})^{h})\cdot(1-(t^{m_{1}}+t^{m_{2}}+\cdots t^{m_{s}})) \notag \\
 &= (\sum_{h=1}^{\infty}\,t^{h(r-1)+m_{1}})+(\sum_{h=1}^{\infty}\,t^{h(r-1)+m_{2}})+\cdots+(\sum_{h=1}^{\infty}\,t^{h(r-1)+m_{s}}) \notag \\
 &=  \sum_{k=1}^{s}\sum_{h=1}^{\infty}\,t^{h(r-1)+m_{k}}. \notag 
\end{align}
\noindent Recall that the Hopf algebra $T(V')=UL(V')$. By \cite[Lemma~3.12, Lemma~3.13, p.~132]{CMN1979}, we see that $$Q(A')=Q(UL(V'))=Q(T(V'))=V'$$ is a free 
$T(v)$-module  with $v$ acting on $V'$ by 
$\mathrm{ad}^{i} (v)(-)$.  Then, $V'$ has $\mathrm{ad}^{i} (v)(u_{k})\; ( i\geq0,\; 1\leq k\leq s)$ as a $\mathbb{Z}/p$-basis.

title: Corollary
body_md:
Let  $V=\mathrm{Span}_{\mathbb{Z}/p}\{  u_{1},u_{2},\cdots,u_{s},v\} $ with $1\leq |u_{i}|\leq |v|$  be given. Then there exists an isomorphism of Hopf algebras,\[    T(V)\boxed{}_{T(v)}\mathbb{Z}/p\cong T(\{ \mathrm{ad}^{i} (v)(u_{k})\;|\; i\geq0,\; 1\leq k\leq s\} ).\]
   \noindent Here, the $T(v)$-comodule structure of $T(V)$  is given by the Hopf algebra map $T(V)\rightarrow T(V)\otimes T(v)$, $u_{i}\mapsto u_{i}\otimes1$, $v\mapsto v\otimes1+1\otimes v$.   \hfill $\boxed{}$

label: aminq
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{aminq} For the functor $\mathrm{A}^{\mathrm{min}}\in \mathrm{Fun}(\mathbf{Vect}_{\mathbb{Z}/p}^{0},\mathbf{Coalg}_{\mathbb{Z}/p}),$ the functor $\mathrm{B}^{\mathrm{max}}\in \mathrm{Fun}(\mathbf{Vect}_{\mathbb{Z}/p}^{0},\mathbf{Hop}_{\mathbb{Z}/p})$, together with  functors $$\mathrm{Q}_{n}^{\mathrm{max}}\in\mathrm{Fun}(\mathbf{Vect}_{\mathbb{Z}/p}^{0},\mathbf{Vect}_{\mathbb{Z}/p}^{0})\;\, (n\geq2)$$ constructed by Selick-Wu,    the following assertions hold.

body_md:
\label{btmpro}   Let $n\geq2$ and    $D_{n}=(12\cdots n)\in \mathcal{S}_{n},$ the cycle of length $n$. Hence $D_{n}\in \mathcal{S}_{n}^{op}.$ The following assertions hold.

\begin{itemize}
    \item [\rm (1)]  \begin{itemize}
        \item[\rm (i)] 
     Define the Dynkin-Specht-Wever elements $\beta_{n}\in\mathbb{Z} [\mathcal{S}_{n}]\subseteq \mathbb{Z}_{(p)} [\mathcal{S}_{n}]\subseteq \mathbb{Q}[\mathcal{S}_{n}]$ as follows: $$\beta_{n}=(1-D_{n})(1-D_{n-1})\cdots (1-D_{2});$$
\noindent
    that is, $$\beta_{2}=1-D_{2},\;\beta_{n}=(1-D_{n})\beta_{n-1}=\beta_{n-1}-D_{n}\beta_{n-1}.$$
 \noindent Then, $\beta_{n}\beta_{n}=n\beta_{n}.$  Let  $V$  be an ungraded $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space  and let $ \mathcal{S}_{n}$    act on $V^{\otimes n}$ from the left by permuting factors. Then the  action of $\beta_{n}$ on $V^{\otimes n}$  is given by $$\beta_{n} (a_{1}a_{2}\cdots a_{n})=[[\cdots[a_{1}, a_{2}], \cdots],  a_{n}], \;\;(a_{i}\in V),$$
the ungraded $n$-fold left-normed Lie bracket.
\item[\rm (ii)] Whether  regarded as elements of  $\mathbb{Q}[\mathcal{S}_{n}]$  or $\mathbb{Q}[\mathcal{S}_{n}^{op}]$, the following elements are  idempotent,
$$\frac{1}{n} (1-D_{n})(1-D_{n-1})\cdots (1-D_{2}),\qquad\frac{1}{n} (1-D_{n}^{-1})(1-D_{n-1}^{-1})\cdots (1-D_{2}^{-1}),$$
$$\frac{1}{n} (1-D_{2})(1-D_{3})\cdots (1-D_{n}),\qquad\frac{1}{n} (1-D_{2}^{-1})(1-D_{3}^{-1})\cdots (1-D_{n}^{-1}).$$\noindent Their 
$n$-multiples lying in $\mathbb{Z}[\mathcal{S}_{n}]$ or $\mathbb{Z}[\mathcal{S}_{n}^{op}]$ are   called  Dynkin-Specht-Wever elements. (This is why some references on $\mathrm{A}^{\min}$-theory define their ``\,$\beta_n$'' to be $(1-D_n^{-1})(1-D_{n-1}^{-1})\cdots(1-D_2^{-1})\in \mathbb{Z}[\mathcal{S}_{n}]$.)
\end{itemize} 
\item [\rm (2)] Let $X\in\mathbf{hCW}_{(p)}^{0}.$ Take the maps $|| \beta_{n} ||' \in [\Sigma X^{\wedge n}, \Sigma X^{\wedge n}]$  as follows: $$ ||\beta_{2}||'=\mathrm{id}_{\Sigma X}+\Sigma \underline{D_{2}}\circ [-1],\;||\beta_{n}||'= ||\beta_{n-1}||'\wedge \mathrm{id}_{X}+ \big(( \Sigma \,\underline{D_{n}}\, )  \circ (||\beta_{n-1}||'\wedge \mathrm{id}_{X})\big)\circ[-1].  $$
Then, $|| \beta_{n} ||'_{*}=|| \beta_{n} ||_{*}\in\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Vect}_{\mathbb{Z}/p}^{0}} (\widetilde{H}_{*} (\Sigma X^{\wedge n} ),\widetilde{H}_{*} (\Sigma X^{\wedge n} ) ).$ 
 
    \item [\rm (3)] Write $V=\widetilde{H}_{*} ( X )$ and so 
    $\sigma (V^{\otimes n})=\widetilde{H}_{*} (\Sigma X^{\wedge n} )$. Suppose $a_{i}\in V$. Then the action of $\beta_{n}$ on homology  is given by\\\centerline{$|| \beta_{n} ||_{*}\colon \sigma (V^{\otimes n})\longrightarrow \sigma (V^{\otimes n})$,\qquad\quad\qquad\quad\qquad\quad\qquad\quad}$$\sigma (a_{1}a_{2}\cdots a_{n})\mapsto\sigma[[\cdots[a_{1}, a_{2}], \cdots],  a_{n}],$$
\noindent $(\text{the}\;\sigma\text{-image of the}\; n\text{-fold left-normed Lie bracket} ).$ 



\item [\rm (4)] Use the notation of (3).  Let $\iota=\mathrm{id}_{X}$  and $W_{n}=[[\cdots[\iota, \iota], \cdots],  \iota]\in[\Sigma X^{\wedge n},\Sigma X]$, the left-normed Whitehead product. Further suppose that all elements in $V=\widetilde{H}_{*} (X)$ are primitive. 
Then, at the homology  level, $(\Omega W_{n})_{*}\colon H_{*} (\Omega\Sigma X^{\wedge n})\rightarrow H_{*} (\Omega\Sigma X)$  is given by \\\\\centerline{\;\;\qquad$ (\Omega W_{n})_{*}\colon T (V^{\otimes n})\longrightarrow T (V)$,\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad\qquad\quad\qquad\qquad}$$ \;a_{1}a_{2}\cdots a_{n}\mapsto[[\cdots[a_{1}, a_{2}], \cdots],  a_{n}],\;(a_{i}\in V).$$

Accordingly, we write  $(\Omega W_{n})_{*} (a_{1}a_{2}\cdots a_{n})=\beta_{n} (a_{1}a_{2}\cdots a_{n})$.
\end{itemize}

title: Proof
body_md:
\begin{itemize}
 \item [\rm (1)] These results are well-known in representation theory. They, or equivalent formulations of them, were proved independently by Dynkin \cite{Dynkin} 
in 1947, Specht \cite{Specht}  in 1948 and Wever \cite{Wever}  in 1949. None of their original papers is available in English. For readers in algebraic topology, we briefly explain why these results hold.

\indent \quad An English reference containing a proof  that $\frac{1}{n} (1-D_{2}^{-1})(1-D_{3}^{-1})\cdots (1-D_{n}^{-1})\in \mathbb{Q}[S_{n}^{op}]$ is idempotent is given in Reutenauer's book \cite[Theorem 8.16, p.~195]{btn}.  Moreover, this theorem  shows that the linear transformation  $\mathscr{A}$, $$(\mathbb{Q}^{\oplus n})^{\otimes n}\stackrel{\mathscr{A}}\longrightarrow(\mathbb{Q}^{\oplus n})^{\otimes n},\;\;x_{1}x_{2}\cdots x_{n}\mapsto \frac{1}{n}[[\cdots[x_{1}, x_{2}], \cdots],  x_{n}], (x_{i}\in\mathbb{Q}^{\oplus n})$$
\noindent is idempotent. We now explain why the remaining elements listed in (ii) are idempotent.
Notice that there exists a ring  isomorphism   $\mathbb{Q}[\mathcal{S}_{n}]\xrightarrow[]{-1}\mathbb{Q}[\mathcal{S}_{n}^{op}]$ determined by $\tau\in \mathcal{S}_{n}\mapsto \tau^{-1}\in \mathcal{S}^{op}_{n}$, and a ring anti-automorphism   $\mathbb{Q}[\mathcal{S}_{n}]\xrightarrow[]{-1}\mathbb{Q}[\mathcal{S}_{n}]$ determined by $\tau\in \mathcal{S}_{n}\mapsto \tau^{-1}\in \mathcal{S}_{n}$. Then it is easy to see  that 
\begin{align}
&\qquad\;\frac{1}{n} (1-D_{n})(1-D_{n-1})\cdots (1-D_{2})\in\mathbb{Q}[\mathcal{S}_{n}^{op}]\text{\;is idempotent} \notag \\
 &\Longleftrightarrow \frac{1}{n} (1-D_{n}^{-1})(1-D_{n-1}^{-1})\cdots (1-D_{2}^{-1})\in\mathbb{Q}[\mathcal{S}_{n}^{}]\text{\;is idempotent} \notag \\
 &\Longleftrightarrow \frac{1}{n} (1-D_{2})(1-D_{3})\cdots (1-D_{n})\in\mathbb{Q}[\mathcal{S}_{n}]\text{\;is idempotent} \notag \\
 &\Longleftrightarrow\frac{1}{n} (1-D_{2}^{-1})(1-D_{3}^{-1})\cdots (1-D_{n}^{-1})\in\mathbb{Q}[\mathcal{S}_{n}^{op}]\text{\;is idempotent}.\notag 
\end{align}
\noindent Thus, all four elements above are idempotent. It also follows easily that 
\begin{align}
&\qquad\;\frac{1}{n} (1-D_{n})(1-D_{n-1})\cdots (1-D_{2})\in\mathbb{Q}[\mathcal{S}_{n}]\text{\;is idempotent} \notag \\
 &\Longleftrightarrow \frac{1}{n} (1-D_{n}^{-1})(1-D_{n-1}^{-1})\cdots (1-D_{2}^{-1})\in\mathbb{Q}[\mathcal{S}_{n}^{op}]\text{\;is idempotent} \notag \\
 &\Longleftrightarrow \frac{1}{n} (1-D_{2})(1-D_{3})\cdots (1-D_{n})\in\mathbb{Q}[\mathcal{S}_{n}^{op}]\text{\;is idempotent} \notag \\
 &\Longleftrightarrow\frac{1}{n} (1-D_{2}^{-1})(1-D_{3}^{-1})\cdots (1-D_{n}^{-1})\in\mathbb{Q}[\mathcal{S}_{n}]\text{\;is idempotent}.\notag 
\end{align}
\noindent

















 Note that the  representation $R$ arising from the left  permutation action of $\mathcal{S}_{n}$ on the tensor factors
\[
\mathbb{Q}[\mathcal{S}_n]\stackrel{R}\longrightarrow \mathrm{Hom}\bigl((\mathbb{Q}^{\oplus n})^{\otimes n},(\mathbb{Q}^{\oplus n})^{\otimes n}\bigr)
\] \noindent is  faithful. Moreover, by induction on $n$, one obtains that  $\frac{1}{n}\beta_{n}=\frac{1}{n} (1-D_{n})(1-D_{n-1})\cdots (1-D_{2})\in\mathbb{Q}[\mathcal{S}_{n}]$ also gives \text{the linear transformation } $$ (\mathbb{Q}^{\oplus n})^{\otimes n}\stackrel{\mathscr{A}}\longrightarrow(\mathbb{Q}^{\oplus n})^{\otimes n},\quad x_{1}x_{2}\cdots x_{n}\mapsto \frac{1}{n}[[\cdots[x_{1}, x_{2}], \cdots],  x_{n}],\;(x_{i}\in\mathbb{Q}^{\oplus n})$$ 
\noindent  under the  representation $R$. 
(To see this, it suffices to treat  $x_{1}x_{2}\cdots x_{n-1}\in (\mathbb{Q}^{\oplus n})^{\otimes (n-1)}$
 as a single block $X_{n-1}$. Then $D_{n}=(12\cdots n)$   swaps the block $X_{n-1}$  and the tensor factor $x_{n}\in(\mathbb{Q}^{\oplus n})^{\otimes 1}$. That is,  $D_{n} (X_{n-1}x_{n})=x_{n}X_{n-1}$.) Since the linear transformation $\mathscr{A}$ is idempotent and the representation $R$ is faithful, we infer that $\frac{1}{n}\beta_{n}$ is idempotent, and hence the other four elements listed above  are idempotent as well. That is,   Reutenauer's theorem \cite[Theorem 8.16, p.~195]{btn} essentially shows that  all the elements  listed in (ii) are idempotent. (The element $\beta_{n}$ is usually denoted by $\omega_{n}$  in representation theory. We  follow the convention of Fred Cohen. Note that $\omega_{n}$ stands for the Whitehead product $[\mathrm{id}_{S^n},\mathrm{id}_{S^n}]$ in homotopy theory.) 
   \item [\rm (2)] It follows from  (1) and the definition  of the notation $|| \beta_{n}||$, see Equation (\ref{el}).
   \item [\rm (3)]
  For convenience, we omit the homology suspension isomorphism from the notation $\sigma$ in this proof  if no confusion arises. Note that $\underline{D_{2}}=\underline{(12)}$, the switching map.   At the homology level, $\underline{D_{2}}_{*} (a_{1}a_{2})=(-1)^{|a_{1}||a_{2}|}a_{2}a_{1}.$ Hence, \[
\beta_2(a_{1}a_{2}) =a_{1} a_{2} - (-1)^{|a_{1}||a_{2}|} a_{2}a_{1}=[a_{1},a_{2}].\]

Assume that $$\beta_{n-1} (a_{1}a_{2}\cdots a_{n-1})=[[\cdots[a_{1}, a_{2}], \cdots],  a_{n-1}].$$ We show that $$\beta_{n} (a_{1}a_{2}\cdots a_{n})=[[\cdots[a_{1}, a_{2}], \cdots],  a_{n-1}] a_{n}-(-1)^{r}a_{n}[[\cdots[a_{1}, a_{2}], \cdots],  a_{n-1}],$$
where $r=|[[\cdots[a_{1}, a_{2}], \cdots],  a_{n-1}]|\cdot |a_{n}|$; that is, we  need to show that $$\beta_{n} (a_{1}a_{2}\cdots a_{n})=[[\cdots[a_{1}, a_{2}], \cdots],  a_{n}].$$ By the assumption and the relation  $||\beta_{n}||'= ||\beta_{n-1}||'\wedge \mathrm{id}_{X}+ \big(( \Sigma \,\underline{D_{n}}\, )  \circ (||\beta_{n-1}||'\wedge \mathrm{id}_{X})\big)\circ[-1]$ given in (2), we have $$\beta_{n} (a_{1}a_{2}\cdots a_{n})=[[\cdots[a_{1}, a_{2}], \cdots],  a_{n-1}] a_{n}-\underline{D_{n}}_{*}\big([[\cdots[a_{1}, a_{2}], \cdots],  a_{n-1}] a_{n}\big).$$

Thus we need only to show that \begin{equation}\label{gnjs}
    \underline{D_{n}}_{*}\big([[\cdots[a_{1}, a_{2}], \cdots],  a_{n-1}] \otimes a_{n}\big)=(-1)^{r}a_{n}\otimes[[\cdots[a_{1}, a_{2}], \cdots],  a_{n-1}].
\end{equation}  Recall that $D_{n}=(12\cdots n)$. Therefore $$\underline{D_{n}} (x_{1}\wedge x_{2}\wedge\cdots \wedge x_{n})=x_{n}\wedge x_{1}\wedge x_{2}\wedge\cdots \wedge x_{n-1},\;(x_{i}\in X).$$ Then Equation (\ref{gnjs})  follows from the commutative diagram, \begin{equation}\label{gy123}
    \begin{tikzcd}
X^{\wedge n}\arrow[r,"\underline{D_{n}}"] \arrow[d, equal] & X^{\wedge n} \arrow[d, equal] \\
X^{\wedge (n-1)}\wedge X \arrow[r, "\tau"]                           & X\wedge X^{\wedge (n-1)}.\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}
\noindent
Here, $\tau$ denotes the switching map $(x_{1}\wedge x_{2}\wedge\cdots \wedge x_{n-1})\wedge x_{n} \mapsto x_{n}\wedge (x_{1}\wedge x_{2}\wedge\cdots \wedge x_{n-1})$.






\item[\rm (4)] Essentially, we have proved this assertion in Lemma \ref{samelson}. Note that here we write $a\otimes b$ as $ab$ for short. For $n=2$, the result follows from Lemma \ref{samelson} (2).
For $n\geq3$, apply Lemma \ref{samelson} (3) through taking the map $f_{1}=\langle \cdots \langle E, E\rangle,\cdots , E\rangle$ ($(n-1)$-fold) and the map $f_{2}=E$. It is not hard to obtain the result   by induction  on $n$. 
\end{itemize}

\mathrm{A}^{\mathrm{min}} (S^{2i-1})\simeq S^{2i-1} \quad \text{and}\quad
\mathrm{B}^{\mathrm{max}} (S^{2i-1})\simeq \Omega S^{4i-1}.
\]

The second row gives  Serre's odd primary splitting, $\Omega S^{2i}\simeq S^{2i-1}\times \Omega S^{4i-1}$.
\end{itemize}

title: Proof
body_md:
Notice that  $H_{*} (\Omega\Sigma S^{n})\cong T(x)$ as Hopf algebras where $|x|=n$. Let  $V=\widetilde{H}_{*} (S^{n})=\mathrm{span}_{\mathbb{Z}/p}\{  x\} .$
\begin{itemize}
\item[\rm(1)]   Recall the properties given by Proposition~\ref{aminq} (2) and (5). In this case, $L_{n} (V)=0$ for all $n\geq2$ and hence $$0=L_{n} (V)\supseteq \mathrm{Q}_{n}^{\mathrm{max}} (V),$$ leading to $\mathrm{Q}_{n}^{\mathrm{max}} (V)=0$ for all $n\geq2$. Then $\mathrm{SQ}_{n}^{\mathrm{max}} (S^{i})\simeq*$ for all $n\geq2.$
The remaining part follows from Proposition~\ref{amindl} (1).
 \item[\rm(2)] For the even case, the proof is similar to that part (1).   We consider  the odd case, setting $n=2i-1$.
Clearly, in $T(x)$, $$[x,x]=2x^{2},\;[[x,x],x]=[2x^{2},x]=0.$$


\noindent Thus, $L_{2} (V)=\mathrm{Span}_{\mathbb{Z}/p}\{  2 x^{2}\} ,\; (|2 x^{2}|=2n=4i-2)$ and $L_{j} (V)=0$, ($j\geq3$). By Equation (\ref{tdgs}), we have $$\widetilde{H}_{*} (\mathrm{SQ}_{2}^{\max} (S^{2i-1}))=\sigma L_{2} (V)=\mathrm{Span}_{\mathbb{Z}/p}\{  2\sigma x^{2}\} ,\;\;|2\sigma x^{2}|=4i-1,$$$$\widetilde{H}_{*} (\mathrm{SQ}_{j}^{\max} (S^{2i-1}))\subseteq \sigma L_{j} (V)=0,\;\;j\geq3.$$
\noindent
Then, $\mathrm{SQ}_{2}^{\max} (S^{2i-1})\simeq S^{4i-1}$, $\mathrm{SQ}_{j}^{\max} (S^{2i-1})\simeq *$ for all $j\geq3.$ So, $\mathrm{B}^{\max} (S^{2i-1})=\Omega\bigvee_{n\geq2}\mathrm{SQ}_{n}^{\max} (S^{2i-1})\simeq\Omega S^{4i-1}.$ It follows that $$\Omega\Sigma S^{2i-1}\simeq \mathrm{A}^{\min} (S^{2i-1})\times\Omega S^{4i-1} \,\;\text{for all}\;\,i\geq1.$$

\noindent Applying $H_{*} (-)$, we have $H_{2i-1} (\mathrm{A}^{\min} (S^{2i-1}))\cong\mathbb{Z}/p$ and  $\widetilde{H}_{\ell} (\mathrm{A}^{\min} (S^{2i-1}))=0$
 for all $\ell\neq 2i-1$.
\noindent Applying $\pi_{*} (-)$, we have $\pi_{2i-1} (\mathrm{A}^{\min} (S^{2i-1}))\cong\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$ and $\pi_{\ell} (\mathrm{A}^{\min} (S^{2i-1}))=0$ for all $\ell<2i-1$. Hence,  we obtain $$\mathrm{A}^{\min} (S^{2i-1})\simeq S^{2i-1}\,\;\text{for all}\;\,i\geq2.$$ In the case $i=1$,  $\mathrm{A}^{\min} (S^{2i-1})=\mathrm{A}^{\min} (S^{1})$ is not simply-connected. Nevertheless, we  have the decomposition  $\Omega S^{2}\simeq\mathrm{A}^{\min} (S^{1})\times\Omega S^{3}$. By employing the Hopf fibration $S^{1}\rightarrow S^{3}\rightarrow S^{2}$ and the fact $\pi_{\bullet\geq2} (S^{1})=0$, we have $\pi_{j} (\Omega S^{3})\cong\pi_{j} (\Omega S^{2})$ for all $j\geq2$. Since homotopy groups of spheres are finitely generated, we infer $\pi_{j} (\mathrm{A}^{\min} (S^{1}))=0$ for all $j\geq2$. In summary, we have $\pi_{1} (\mathrm{A}^{\min} (S^{1}))\cong\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$ and $\pi_{j} (\mathrm{A}^{\min} (S^{1}))=0$ for all $j\neq1$. Hence, $\mathrm{A}^{\min} (S^{1})\simeq S^{1}.$


 
\end{itemize}

Recall that 
$\mathrm{B}^{\mathrm{max}} (X)=\Omega\bigvee_{m\geq2} \mathrm{SQ}^{\mathrm{max}}_{m} (X)$ and that $\mathrm{SQ}^{\mathrm{max}}_{m} (S^{i})$ is simply-connected for each $m\geq2$ and $i\geq1$. Let $i\colon F\rightarrow \Sigma C_{f}$ be the homotopy fiber inclusion.

Proposition~\ref{amindl} (1), we have

label: q3max
title: Lemma
body_md: \label{q3max}Suppose that the prime $p\neq3$. Then  $\mathrm{SQ}_{3}^{\mathrm{max}} (C_{f})\simeq\Sigma^{2n+k+2}C_{f}.$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $X=C_{f}=S^{n}\cup e^{n+k+1}$ and so $\widetilde{H}_{*} (X)=\mathrm{Span}_{\mathbb{Z}/p}\{  x,y\} $,
where $|x|=n,\;  |y|=n+k+1$.  Then,
according to Proposition \ref{tl}, 
there is a map $g: S^{|x|}\wedge S^{|y|}\rightarrow X\wedge X$ such that $$g_{*} (\iota_{|x|+|y|})=xy+tyx\in H_{|x|+|y|} (X\wedge X)$$ for some  integer $t\in [1,p-1].$ Recall that $\mathrm{SQ}_{3}^{\mathrm{max}} (X)=\mathrm{hocolim(}\Sigma X^{ \wedge 3}\stackrel{\beta_{3}/3\;}\longrightarrow\Sigma X^{ \wedge 3}\stackrel{\beta_{3}/3\;}\longrightarrow\cdots).$ Let $\phi_{2}$ be the canonical map from the second $\Sigma X^{ \wedge 3}$ in the sequence to $\mathrm{SQ}_{3}^{\mathrm{max}} (X)$. 
Consider the composition $\Psi$, $$ \Psi\colon(\emph{S}^{1}\wedge X)\wedge (S^{|x|}\wedge S^{|y|})\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{id}\wedge g} (S^{1}\wedge X)\wedge (X\wedge X)\xrightarrow[]{\beta_{3}/3} S^{1}\wedge X\wedge X\wedge X\xrightarrow[]{\phi_{2}}\mathrm{SQ}_{3}^{\mathrm{max}} (X). $$
Applying $\widetilde{H}_{*} (-),$ we get 
$$ \Psi_{*}\colon\widetilde{H}_{*} (S^{1}\wedge X)\otimes \widetilde{H}_{*}  (S^{|x|}\wedge S^{|y|})\xrightarrow[]{\mathrm{id}\otimes g_{*}} \widetilde{H}_{*} (S^{1}\wedge X)\otimes \widetilde{H}_{*} (X\wedge X)\xrightarrow[]{\beta_{3}/3} \widetilde{H}_{*} (S^{1}\wedge X\wedge X\wedge X)\xrightarrow[]{\phi_{2*}}\widetilde{H}_{*} (\mathrm{SQ}_{3}^{\mathrm{max}} (X)). $$

\noindent Suppose $a\in \widetilde{H}_{*} (X)$. We examine the value of $(\sigma a)\iota_{|x|+|y|}$ under $\Psi_{*}$. By  
Proposition \ref{btmpro} (3) and fact (\ref{ps2}), we infer that
$$\Psi_{*}\colon (\sigma a)\iota_{|x|+|y|}\stackrel{\mathrm{id}\otimes g_{*}}\longmapsto(\sigma a) (xy+tyx)\stackrel{\beta_{3}/3}\longmapsto\frac{1}{3}\sigma([[a,x],y]+t[[a,y],x])\stackrel{\phi_{2*}}\longmapsto\frac{1}{3}\sigma([[a,x],y]+t[[a,y],x]). $$
\noindent Hence, $$\Psi_{*} ((\sigma x)\iota_{|x|+|y|})=\frac{t}{3}\sigma([[x,y],x]),\quad\Psi_{*} ((\sigma y)\iota_{|x|+|y|})=\frac{t}{3}\sigma([[y,x],y])=\pm \frac{t}{3}\sigma([[x,y],y]).$$
\noindent (We use the symbols $\frac{t}{3}$ and $\frac{1}{3}$ by employing the obvious $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$-module structure of the $\mathbb{Z}/p$-vector space.) So, $$\mathrm{Im} (\Psi_{*})=\widetilde{H}_{*} (\mathrm{SQ}_{3}^{\mathrm{max}} (X)).$$  \noindent Noting that the domain and codomain of $\Psi_{*}$ are vector spaces of dimension 2, we deduce that $\Psi_{*}$ is an isomorphism. 
By the $p$-local Whitehead theorem, we know that $$\Psi\colon (S^{1}\wedge X)\wedge (S^{|x|}\wedge S^{|y|})\rightarrow \mathrm{SQ}_{3}^{\mathrm{max}} (X)$$ \noindent
is a homotopy equivalence.

body_md: \label{pxlmb} Let $m\geq0.$ In the $\mathbb{Z}/p$-homology Leray-Serre spectral sequence associated with the homotopy fibration $\Omega F\rightarrow*\rightarrow F$,  we have $\tau(ab^{m})=\mathrm{ad}^{m} (y)(x)\; $ up to a unit in $\mathbb{Z}/p$, where $\tau$ denotes the transgression. title: Proof
body_md:
Consider the $\mathbb{Z}/p$-homology Leray-Serre spectral sequence $\{  E^{\bullet}_{\bullet,\bullet},d_{\bullet}\} $ associated with the homotopy fibration  $\Omega F\rightarrow*\rightarrow F$ and apply Proposition \ref{mdpxl}. Observe that $$E^{2}_{0,*}=H_{*} (\Omega F)= T(\{ \mathrm{ad}^{m} (y)(x)\;|\; m\geq0\} ),\;\;(|x|=n,\; |y|=n+k+1),$$
    $$E^{2}_{*,0}=H_{*} ( F)= \mathrm{Span}_{\mathbb{Z}/p}\{  ab^{m}\;|\;m\geq0\} ,\;\;(|a|=n+1,\;|b|=n+k+2).$$
    \noindent  In the following, ``$=$" stands for being equal up to  a unit in $\mathbb{Z}/p$.  The relations $$d(a)=x=\mathrm{ad}^{0} (y)(x), \;d(a\cdot\alpha)=x\alpha, \;(a\cdot\alpha\in E^{n}_{n,\bullet},\;\; \alpha\in E^{2}_{0,\bullet})$$\noindent in the $E^{n}$-page
   force $d(ab)=[x,y]=\mathrm{ad}^{1} (y)(x)$ in the 
   $E^{2n+k+3}$-page. The relations $$d(ab)=\mathrm{ad}^{1} (y)(x),\;d(ab\cdot\alpha)=(\mathrm{ad}^{1} (y)(x))\alpha, \;(ab\cdot\alpha\in E^{2n+k+1}_{2n+k+1,\bullet},\;\; \alpha\in E^{2}_{0,\bullet})$$ in the 
   $E^{2n+k+3}$-page imply $d(ab^{2})=\mathrm{ad}^{2} (y)(x)$ in the 
   $E^{3n+2k+5}$-page. It is not hard to obtain $d(ab^{m})=\mathrm{ad}^{m} (y)(x)$ for all $m$ by induction.

label: lof2
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\begin{itemize}
    \item[\rm(1)]
     Consider the $\mathbb{Z}/p$-homology Leray-Serre spectral sequence $\{  E^{\bullet}_{\bullet,\bullet},d_{\bullet}\} $ associated with the homotopy fibration $\Omega F^{(2)}\rightarrow*\rightarrow F^{(2)}$. Recall that it is a  $H_{*} (\Omega F^{(2)})$-module spectral sequence,  $d(u v)=(du) v$ where $u\in E_{\bullet,0}^{\bullet}$ and $v\in E_{0,\bullet}^{2}$, (see Proposition \ref{mdpxl}). Notice that the pair $(\Omega F, \OmegaF^{(2)})$ is $((3n+2k+2)-1)$-connected. Thus we have
     $H_{\bullet\leq s} (\OmegaF^{(2)})\subseteq H_{\bullet\leq s} (\Omega F)$ where $s=|[x,y]|$. Additionally, $(\Omega i)_{*}$ is a Hopf algebra homomorphism. Combining with the algebra structure of  $H_{*} (\Omega F)$, we infer that in $H_{*} (\OmegaF^{(2)})$, every monomial of the form $$x^{i_{1}} [x,y]^{i_{2}}x^{i_{3}} [x,y]^{i_{4}}\cdots x^{i_{t}} [x,y]^{i_{t+1}}$$ is nonzero where the numbers $i_{\bullet}$ denote non-negative  integers. Then, a calculation following the  method in the proof of Lemma \ref{pxlmb} shows that $H_{*} (\OmegaF^{(2)})\cong T(x, [x,y])$ as  algebras. To show  $x, [x,y]\in H_{*} (\OmegaF^{(2)})$ are primitive, notice that $\OmegaF^{(2)}\rightarrow\Omega F$ induces a monomorphism of tensor algebras (thereby of Hopf algebras) and $x, [x,y]\in H_{*} (\Omega F)$ are primitive. \item [\rm(2)] The proof is similar to (1).  Set $w=[[x,y],y]$. Since $F^{(3)}=\mathrm{sk}_{4n+3k+3} (F)$, we see that the pair $(F,F^{(3)})$ is $((4n+3k+4)-1)$-connected. Hence the pair $(\Omega F,\Omega F^{(3)})$ is $((4n+3k+3)-1)$-connected. In particular,
\[
H_{\bullet\le |w|} (\Omega F^{(3)}) \xrightarrow[]{\cong}
H_{\bullet\le |w|} (\Omega F),
\qquad |w|=|[[x,y],y]|.
\]
Therefore the elements $x,[x,y],w\in H_{*} (\Omega F)$ determine elements with the same names in $H_{*} (\Omega F^{(3)})$. Consider the $\mathbb{Z}/p$-homology Leray-Serre spectral sequence
$\{  E^{\bullet}_{\bullet,\bullet},d_\bullet\} $
associated with the homotopy fibration
$\Omega F^{(3)}\rightarrow * \rightarrow F^{(3)}.$ As in assertion \rm(1), this is a  $H_{*} (\Omega F^{(3)})$-module spectral sequence. Combining with the above information, a calculation parallel to that in the proof of Lemma~\ref{pxlmb} shows that $H_{*} (\Omega F^{(3)})\cong T(x,[x,y],w)$ as algebras. Finally, the inclusion $\Omega F^{(3)}\rightarrow \Omega F$ induces a monomorphism of Hopf algebras. Since the images of $x,[x,y],w$ in $H_{*} (\Omega F)$ are primitive, it follows that $x,[x,y],w$ are primitive in $H_{*} (\Omega F^{(3)})$ as well. Therefore,  $H_{*} (\Omega F^{(3)})\cong T(x,[x,y],[[x,y],y])$ as Hopf algebras.\end{itemize}

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{410} Let $\mathrm{d}=\mathrm{rank} (\mathbb{Z}/p\otimes \mathrm{Im} (q_{2*}))$, the number of  the direct summands of $$\mathrm{Im} (q_{2*})=\mathrm{Im}\big(q_{2*}\colon\pi_{3n+k+2} (F^{(2)})\rightarrow \pi_{3n+k+2} (S^{2n+k+2})= \Sigma\pi_{3n+k+1} (S^{2n+k+1}) \big),$$ and  let  $\{ \Sigma\mathbbm{y}^{(i)} \} _{ 1\leq i\leq \mathrm{d}} $ be  an  arbitrary minimal generating set of $\mathrm{Im} (q_{2*})$. Take  $$[\Sigma\mathbbm{y}^{(i)}]\in\{  j_{2.5},\;[\iota_{n+1},\Sigma f],\;\mathbbm{y}^{(i)} \} \subseteq \mathrm{Coext}_{[\iota_{n+1},\Sigma f]} (\Sigma\mathbbm{y}^{(i)})\subseteq \pi_{3n+k+2} (F^{(2)}).$$ The  element $[\Sigma\mathbbm{y}^{(i)}]$ is in fact both a lift of $-\Sigma\mathbbm{y}^{(i)}$ and  a coextension of $\mathbbm{y}^{(i)}$ for each $i$ if $\mathrm{d}\geq1$. Then, 
    $\pi_{3n+k+1} (\OmegaF^{(2)})$ is generated by $$\text{elements lying in}\;(\Omega j_{2.5})\circ \pi_{3n+k+1} (\Omega S^{n+1}),\;\;\text{the element}\;\mathrm{adj} (j_{3}j_{4})=\Omega j_{3}\circ \mathrm{adj} (j_{4})\colon S^{3n+k+1}\rightarrow\OmegaF^{(2)}$$  $$\text{and the elements}\;\;\mathrm{adj} ([\Sigma\mathbbm{y}^{(i)}]),\;(1\leq i\leq \mathrm{d}).$$ 
    
\noindent If \(\mathrm{d}=0\), so that the symbol
$
\{ \Sigma\mathbbm{y}^{(i)} \} _{ 1\leq i\leq \mathrm{d}}$
does not occur, we regard the $[\Sigma\mathbbm{y}^{(i)}], (1\le i\le \mathrm{d}) $
part together with the
$
\mathrm{adj} ([\Sigma\mathbbm{y}^{(i)}]),\, (1\le i\le \mathrm{d})$
part as \(0\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First consider the case $\mathrm{d}\geq1$. We will freely use some classical methods for calculating homotopy groups, see Remark \ref{jssq} for these methods. The homotopy fibering $G=(S^{n+1}\vee S^{3n+k+2})\cup e^{5n+2k+3}\cup\cdots \stackrel{j_{3}}\longrightarrowF^{(2)}\stackrel{q_{2}}\longrightarrow S^{2n+k+2}$ induces an exact sequence \begin{equation}\notag
    \pi_{3n+k+2} (S^{n+1}\vee S^{3n+k+2}) \stackrel{}\longrightarrow\pi_{3n+k+2} (F^{(2)})\stackrel{q_{2*}}\longrightarrow \pi_{3n+k+2} (S^{2n+k+2})\stackrel{\partial}\rightarrow \pi_{3n+k+1} (S^{n+1}),
\end{equation}

\noindent which is canonically identified with the exact sequence
$$\pi_{3n+k+1} (\Omega (S^{n+1}\vee S^{3n+k+2})) \stackrel{}\longrightarrow\pi_{3n+k+1} (\OmegaF^{(2)})\stackrel{(\Omega q_{2})_{*}}\longrightarrow \pi_{3n+k+1} (\Omega S^{2n+k+2})\stackrel{\partial}\rightarrow \pi_{3n+k} (\Omega S^{n+1}).$$
\noindent Obviously, $\pi_{3n+k+2} (S^{2n+k+2})=\Sigma \pi_{3n+k+1} (S^{2n+k+1})$ and $\partial(\Sigma\mathbbm{x})=[\iota_{n+1},\Sigma f]\circ\mathbbm{x}$  for each $\Sigma\mathbbm{x}\in\pi_{3n+k+2} (S^{2n+k+2}).$ Let the elements $\Sigma\mathbbm{y}^{(i)},\;(1\leq i\leq \mathrm{d})$ denote   generators of a minimal generating set of $$\mathrm{Im} (q_{2*})=\mathrm{Im} (q_{2*}\colon\pi_{3n+k+2} (F^{(2)})\rightarrow \pi_{3n+k+2} (S^{2n+k+2}) )=\mathrm{Ker} (\partial)$$ where $\mathrm{d}=\mathrm{rank} (\mathbb{Z}/p\otimes \mathrm{Im} (q_{2*}))\geq1$ by the assumption. Therefore,  the taken element $$[\Sigma\mathbbm{y}^{(i)}]\in\{  j_{2.5},\;[\iota_{n+1},\Sigma f],\;\mathbbm{y}^{(i)} \} \subseteq \mathrm{Coext}_{[\iota_{n+1},\Sigma f]} (\Sigma\mathbbm{y}^{(i)})$$ is a lift of $-\Sigma\mathbbm{y}^{(i)}$  as well as a coextension of $\mathbbm{y}^{(i)}$ for each $i$. So,  $\pi_{3n+k+2} (F^{(2)})$ is generated by $$\text{elements lying in}\;j_{2.5}\circ \pi_{3n+k+2} (S^{n+1}),\;\;\text{the element}\;j_{3}j_{4}\colon S^{3n+k+2}\hookrightarrow S^{n+1}\vee S^{3n+k+2}\rightarrow F^{(2)}$$ \noindent and the elements $[\Sigma\mathbbm{y}^{(i)}],\;(1\leq i\leq \mathrm{d})$.
Equivalently speaking, $\pi_{3n+k+1} (\OmegaF^{(2)})$ is generated by $$\text{elements lying in}\;(\Omega j_{2.5})\circ \pi_{3n+k+1} (\Omega S^{n+1}),\;\;\text{the element}\;\mathrm{adj} (j_{3}j_{4})=\Omega j_{3}\circ \mathrm{adj} (j_{4})\colon S^{3n+k+1}\rightarrow\OmegaF^{(2)}$$ \noindent and the elements $\mathrm{adj} ([\Sigma\mathbbm{y}^{(i)}]),\;(1\leq i\leq \mathrm{d})$. Hence, the result holds when $\mathrm{d}\geq1$. It is easy to see that the result   also holds when $\mathrm{d}=0$.

label: gyts
title: Lemma
body_md: \label{gyts} For the space $F^{(2)}=S^{n+1}\cup _{[\iota_{n+1},\Sigma f]}e^{2n+k+2}$, the graded group $H_{*} (\Omega F^{(2)};\mathbb{Z}_{(p)})$ is $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$-torsion free when $k\geq1$ or $n$ is even.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $k\geq1$ or $n+1$ is odd, then    $H^{*} (F^{(2)};\mathbb{Z}_{(p)})$ is a trivial algebra.  Consider the $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$-cohomology Leray-Serre spectral sequence  $\{  E_{\bullet}^{\bullet,\bullet}, d^{\bullet}\} $ associated with the homotopy fibration $\Omega F^{(2)}\rightarrow *\rightarrow F^{(2)}$. The Leibniz rule and the trivial algebra structure of $H^{*} (F^{(2)};\mathbb{Z}_{(p)})$  imply that $d^{n+1} (u)=0$ for all  $u\in E_{i}^{n+1,j}$ with $i\geq2$ and $j\geq 1$.


Next we show that
 the graded group $H^{*} (\Omega F^{(2)};\mathbb{Z}_{(p)})$ is $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$-torsion  free.  To obtain a contradiction, assume that there exists a nonzero $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$-torsion element $a\in H^{*} (\OmegaF^{(2)};\mathbb{Z}_{(p)})$ with $|a|\geq1$. Then, we can find a nonzero $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$-torsion element $b\in H^{*} (\OmegaF^{(2)};\mathbb{Z}_{(p)})$ with $|b|\geq1$ such that $|b|\leq |a|$ for all nonzero $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$-torsion elements $a\in H^{*} (\OmegaF^{(2)};\mathbb{Z}_{(p)})$. It follows that all elements $v\in E_{r}^{i,j}$ with $j<|b|$,\;$i\geq1$ and $r\geq2$  are $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$-torsion free. Then in each page, $d(b)=0$ and so $b\neq0$ survives to $E_{\infty}^{|b|,0}$. However, all elements in $E_{\infty}^{(\bullet,\bullet)\neq0}$ are trivial, giving a contradiction. Thus, the graded group $H^{*} (\Omega F^{(2)};\mathbb{Z}_{(p)})$ is $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$-torsion  free and hence the graded group $H_{*} (\Omega F^{(2)};\mathbb{Z}_{(p)})$ is $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$-torsion free.

label: tdxwsy
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{tdxwsy} Recall   that $\iota\in H_{3n+k+1} (S^{3n+k+1})\cong\mathbb{Z}/p$ denotes the generator. If $k\geq1$ or $n$ is even, then, at the$\;\mathrm{mod}\, p$-homology level for the maps $S^{3n+k+1}\rightarrow \OmegaF^{(2)}$,  each element lying in  $(\Omega j_{2.5})\circ \pi_{3n+k+1} (\Omega S^{n+1})$ sends $\iota$ to 0,  $\mathrm{adj} (j_{3}j_{4})$ sends $\iota$ to $[[x,y],x]$ up a unit in $\mathbb{Z}/p,$ and 
   each   $\mathrm{adj} ([\Sigma\mathbbm{y}^{(i)}])$ sends $\iota$ to 0.
head: environment

label: l1
title: Proof
body_md:
It was proved that the map $\mathrm{adj} (j_{3}j_{4})$ sends $\iota$ to $[[x,y],x]$ up a unit in $\mathbb{Z}/p$ in Lemma \ref{gyf}. We examine the  behavior of the maps at the $\mathbb{Q}$-homology level.
Let $\mathcal{L} (-)$ be the rationalization functor,  sending $p$-local nilpotent CW complexes to their rationalizations, and sending  $p$-local maps to their rationalizations. Then $\mathcal{L} (\pi_{3n+k+1} (\Omega S^{n+1}))=0$ and hence $\mathcal{L} ((\Omega j_{2.5})\circ\pi_{3n+k+1} (\Omega S^{n+1}))=0$. The elements $\mathbbm{y}_{i}$ are in the stable homotopy group, so all  $\mathcal{L} (\mathbbm{y}_{i})=0$.  Thus, 
\begin{align}
\mathcal{L} ([\Sigma\mathbbm{y}^{(i)}]) 
 &\subseteq \mathcal{L}\{  j_{2.5},\;[\iota_{n+1},\Sigma f],\;\mathbbm{y}^{(i)} \} \label{l1} \\
 &\subseteq \{ \mathcal{L} j_{2.5},\;\mathcal{L}[\iota_{n+1},\Sigma f],\;\mathcal{L}\mathbbm{y}^{(i)}) \} \label{l2} \\
 &=\{ \mathcal{L} j_{2.5},\;\mathcal{L}[\iota_{n+1},\Sigma f],\;0 \}   \notag \\
 &= \mathcal{L} j_{2.5}\circ \mathcal{L} \pi_{3n+k+2} ( S^{n+1})\notag \\
 &= 0.\notag
\end{align}

\noindent Here, the relation ``\,$\subseteq$\,'' between Equation (\ref{l1}) and Equation (\ref{l2}) follows from the equivalent definition of Toda brackets (see Toda \cite[Proposition 1.7, p.~13]{Toda}) and the fact that  $\mathcal{L}$ localizes extensions and coextensions.
\noindent Thus, $\mathcal{L} (\mathrm{adj} ([\Sigma\mathbbm{y}^{(i)}]))=\mathrm{adj} (\mathcal{L} ([\Sigma\mathbbm{y}^{(i)}]))=0.$ Then,  all elements in $(\Omega j_{2.5})\circ\pi_{3n+k+1} (\Omega S^{n+1})$   and 
   all   $\mathrm{adj} ([\Sigma\mathbbm{y}^{(i)}])$  induce trivial homomorphisms  of $\mathbb{Q}$-homology groups. Lemma \ref{gyts} tells us that  $H_{*} (\Omega F^{(2)};\mathbb{Z}_{(p)})$ is $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$-torsion free.
Therefore, all elements in $(\Omega j_{2.5})\circ\pi_{3n+k+1} (\Omega S^{n+1})$   and 
   all   $\mathrm{adj} ([\Sigma\mathbbm{y}^{(i)}])$  induce trivial homomorphisms  of $\mathbb{Z}/p$-homology groups. Hence the result holds.

label: zxkya
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We prove the lemma by the method of undetermined coefficients. Suppose that $$\phi=a+t\mathrm{adj} (j_{3}j_{4})+\Sigma_{i=1}^{\mathrm{d}}\lambda_{i} \mathrm{adj}[\Sigma\mathbbm{y}^{(i)}]$$ \noindent where $a\in (\Omega j_{2.5})\circ \pi_{3n+k+1} (\Omega S^{n+1})$ and $t,\lambda_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}.$


Consider the case  that $k\geq1$ or $n$ is even.  Recall that the fact that $\phi_{*} (\iota)=[[x,y],x]]$ up to a unit in $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$; see Lemma \ref{gyf}.  This fact and Lemma \ref{tdxwsy}   imply that $t\in\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$ is a unit. Take $r=1/t$.


Consider  the case that $k=0$ and $n$ is odd. Recall $n\geq2$ by our global assumption. Hence $n\geq3$ in this case. We know $|[[x,y],x]|=3n+k+1=3n+1$. In $H_{3n+1} (\OmegaF^{(2)})$, all  primitive elements are in $\mathrm{Span}_{\mathbb{Z}/p}\{ [[x,y],x]\} $; see Selick's textbook \cite[Theorem 10.5.2, p.~109]{selickjc} or calculate them directly. So, $(\mathrm{adj}[\Sigma\mathbbm{y}^{(i)}])_{*} (\iota)\in \mathrm{Span}_{\mathbb{Z}/p}\{ [[x,y],x]\} .$ It follows that 
we may choose elements $[\Sigma\mathbbm{y}^{(i)}]'$ satisfying the homomorphisms of the$\;\mathrm{mod}\, p$  homology groups  $$(\mathrm{adj}[\Sigma\mathbbm{y}^{(i)}]')_{*}=0 \;\; \text{and}\;\; [\Sigma\mathbbm{y}^{(i)}]' \equiv [\Sigma\mathbbm{y}^{(i)}]\;\mathrm{mod}\, j_{3}j_{4}.$$ Note that the generators $\mathrm{adj} ([\Sigma\mathbbm{y}^{(i)}])$ of $\pi_{3n+k+1} (\OmegaF^{(2)})$ may be replaced by $\mathrm{adj} ([\Sigma\mathbbm{y}^{(i)}]')$; also note that any element lying in\;$(\Omega j_{2.5})\circ \pi_{3n+1} (\Omega S^{n+1})$ obviously induces trivial homomorphisms of the$\;\mathrm{mod}\, p$ homology groups. Then, we reset $$\phi=a+t\mathrm{adj} (j_{3}j_{4})+\Sigma_{i=1}^{\mathrm{d}}\lambda_{i}' \mathrm{adj}[\Sigma\mathbbm{y}^{(i)}]'$$ \noindent where $a\in (\Omega j_{2.5})\circ \pi_{3n+k+1} (\Omega S^{n+1})$ and $t,\lambda_{i}'\in\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}.$ Thus $t\in\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$ is a unit and we choose $r=1/t$.

label: zdlzm
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{zdlzm}Localize spaces at a prime $p$ such that either $p=2$ with no additional assumption on $n+k$, or  $p\geq5$ and  $n+k$  is additionally assumed to be odd.    Assume that the mod $p$ cohomology  algebra $H^{*} (C_{f})$ is a trivial algebra. Then, the homotopy fiber $F$  of  the pinch map  $ *\not\simeq\Sigma C_{f}=S^{n+1}\cup _{\Sigma f} e^{n+k+2} \xrightarrow[]{pinch} S^{n+k+2}$ ($n\geq2,\;k\geq0$) is given by \[F=F^{(2)}\cup_{\beta}  e^{3n+2k+3}\cup e^{4n+3k+4}  \cdots,\;\;\big(\beta\in\pi_{3n+2k+2} (F^{(2)})\big).\]  
\noindent
For its attaching map $\beta$,  the following relations hold: \\ if $k\geq1$ or $n$ is even, then $$\beta \equiv j_{3}  j_{4}\circ \Sigma^{2n+k+2}f\;\mathrm{mod}\, j_{2.5}\circ \pi_{3n+k+2} (S^{n+1})\circ \Sigma^{2n+k+2}f,\;[\Sigma\mathbbm{y}^{(i)}] \circ\Sigma^{2n+k+2}f, (1\leq i\leq \mathrm{d});$$
\noindent if $k=0$ and $n$ is odd, then
$$\beta \equiv j_{3}  j_{4}\circ \Sigma^{2n+k+2}f\;\mathrm{mod}\, j_{2.5}\circ \pi_{3n+k+2} (S^{n+1})\circ \Sigma^{2n+k+2}f,\;[\Sigma\mathbbm{y}^{(i)}]' \circ\Sigma^{2n+k+2}f, (1\leq i\leq \mathrm{d}).$$\noindent That is, $$\beta \equiv j_{3}  j_{4}\circ \Sigma^{2n+k+2}f\;\mathrm{mod}\, I\circ \Sigma^{2n+k+2}f.$$ \noindent Here,   the principal term $j_{3}  j_{4}\circ \Sigma^{2n+k+2}f$   is  the following composition,   \vspace{-0.85\baselineskip}\;\\\;\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=0.15cm]
		  S^{3n+2k+2}\xrightarrow[]{\Sigma ^{2n+k+2}f} S^{3n+k+2}
		\arrow[r, hook,"j_{4}"]
		& \mathrm{hofib} (F^{(2)} \xrightarrow[]{pinch} S^{2n+k+2})
		\arrow[r, "j_{3}"," \shortstack{\scriptsize homotopy fiber\\\scriptsize inclusion}"'] \arrow[d, equal]  & F^{(2)}\arrow[d, equal]
		\\ & (S^{n+1}\vee S^{3n+k+2})\cup e^{5n+2k+3}\cup\cdots& S^{n+1}\cup_{[\mathrm{id},\Sigma f]}  e^{2n+k+2}.
	\end{tikzcd}\] \noindent  The precise description of the maps $[\Sigma\mathbbm{y}^{(i)}] \circ\Sigma^{2n+k+2}f, (1\leq i\leq \mathrm{d})$ and 
    $[\Sigma\mathbbm{y}^{(i)}]' \circ\Sigma^{2n+k+2}f, (1\leq i\leq \mathrm{d})$  are given in Lemma \ref{410} and Lemma~\ref{zxkya}.

label: asd1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{asd1}  The  homomorphism 
$(j_{3}j_{4})_{*}\colon  \pi_{r} (S^{3n+k+2})\rightarrow\pi_{r} (F^{(2)})$ is injective for each $r\leq4n+2k+1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Recall that $$G=(S^{n+1}\vee S^{3n+k+2})\cup e^{5n+2k+3}\cup\cdots.$$ \noindent Let $j_{3.5}\colon  S^{n+1}\rightarrow G$ be the inclusion and $\partial\colon   \pi_{\bullet+1} (S^{2n+k+2})\rightarrow\pi_{\bullet} (G)$ be the connecting homomorphism with respect to the homotopy fibration $G\rightarrow F^{(2)}\rightarrow S^{2n+k+2}$. It is clear that $\pi_{r+1} (S^{2n+k+2})$ is in the stable range as $r\leq4n+2k+1$. Noticing the well-known formula $\partial(\mathbbm{x}\circ\Sigma\mathbbm{y})=\partial(\mathbbm{x})\circ\mathbbm{y}$ we deduce that $$ \partial\pi_{r} (S^{2n+k+2})=j_{3.5}\circ[\mathrm{id}_{S^{n+1}},\Sigma f]\circ\pi_{r-1} (S^{2n+k+1})\subseteq\mathrm{Im}j_{3.5*}.$$
 The sum of $\mathrm{Im}j_{3.5*}$ and $\mathrm{Im}j_{4*}$ is a direct sum in $\pi_{r} (G)$, so $\mathrm{Im}j_{4*}\cap\mathrm{Im}\partial=0$. Therefore the result holds.

label: midrem
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{midrem} The principal term
$j_{3}j_{4}\circ\Sigma^{2n+k+2}f$
and the indeterminacy term come from rather different geometric sources.   The former comes from the second sphere of 
$G=\mathrm{hofib} (F^{(2)}\to S^{2n+k+2})$,
whereas the latter comes from the bottom sphere of
$G$
together with the lifts in $\pi_{*} (F^{(2)})$. Moreover, after passing to adjoint maps on loop spaces, $j_{3}j_{4}$ induces an isomorphism on mod $p$ homology, whereas every map in $I$ induces the zero homomorphism on mod $p$ homology. Hence, the error term $I$  can not absorb the main term $j_{3}j_{4}$, that is, $j_{3}j_{4}\notin I$. Additionally,    for the orders we have the relation $$\mathrm{ord}(j_{3}j_{4}\circ\Sigma^{2n+k+2}f)\geq \mathrm{ord}(\mathbbm{x})$$ for any $\mathbbm{x}\in I\circ\Sigma^{2n+k+2}f$; notice that the   homomorphism $\pi_{3n+2k+2} (j_{3}j_{4})$ is injective (Lemma \ref{asd1}) and that $\Sigma^{2n+k+2}f$ is of order $p^{m}$ for some integer $m\geq0$ when $k\geq1$ and of order $\infty$  or 1 when $k=0$.

In practice, the indeterminacy term  has no effect on the computability of the homotopy groups $\pi_{*} (\Sigma C_{f})$ when $\beta$ is needed, since we may choose a different generating set for the homotopy group. The skill is similar to changing basis in a vector space. For example, let the vector space $V=\langle u,v\rangle\cong \mathbb{Q}^{2}$, and  suppose that $u' \equiv u \;\mathrm{mod}\, v$.
Then we  have 
$V=\langle u',v\rangle\cong \mathbb{Q}^{2}$.

label: bcd
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{bcd} The homotopy fiber of the pinch map $F^{(3)}\rightarrow S^{3n+2k+3}$  is  given by $$J(M_{F^{(2)}},S^{3n+2k+2})=(F^{(2)}\cup _{\gamma} e^{4n+2k+3})\cup e^{5n+3k+4}\cup\cdots.$$ 
The attaching map $\gamma$ satisfies  $\gamma \equiv j_{3}\circ[j_{3.5},\,j_{4}]\circ\Sigma^{3n+k+2}f\;\mathrm{mod}\,[j_{3}j_{3.5},\;I\circ\Sigma^{2n+k+2}f]$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first introduce the notation. Let $a_{1}\colon   S^{n+1}\rightarrow S^{n+1}\vee S^{3n+k+2}$ and $a_{2}\colon   S^{3n+k+2}\rightarrow S^{n+1}\vee S^{3n+k+2}$ be the inclusions. By the standard technique, we may replace $\beta\colon   S^{3n+k+2}\rightarrowF^{(2)} $  by the inclusion to the mapping cylinder, $i\colon   S^{3n+k+2}\rightarrow M_{\beta}= M_{F^{(2)}}$; let $\bar{j}_{2.5}$ be the composition $ S^{n+1} \xrightarrow[]{j_{2.5}}F^{(2)}\hookrightarrow M_{F^{(2)}}$.  Denote the relative folding map $$ M_{F^{(2)}}\vee S^{3n+k+2}\rightarrow J_{2} (M_{F^{(2)}},S^{3n+2k+2})=M_{F^{(2)}} $$ by $\nabla$, which is given by $\nabla(x,*)=\mathrm{id}_{M_{F^{(2)}}} (x)=x,\;\nabla(*,a)=i(a)=a.$

According to Gray \cite{Gray}, we have a commutative diagram whose  first row is a  homotopy cofibration,\[
\begin{tikzcd}
S^{n+1}\wedge S^{3n+2k+1} \arrow[r,"{[a_{1},a
_{2}]}"] &S^{n+1}\vee S^{3n+2k+2} \arrow[r,"u_{1}", hook] \arrow[d, hook,"\bar{j}_{2.5}\vee \mathrm{id}"'] &S^{n+1}\times  S^{3n+2k+2}\arrow[d,  hook] \\
 & M_{F^{(2)}}\vee S^{3n+2k+2} \arrow[d, "\nabla"']\arrow[r,hook] & M_{F^{(2)}}\times S^{3n+2k+2}\arrow[d, two heads] \\
& J_{2} (M_{F^{(2)}}, S^{3n+2k+2}) \arrow[r, hook] & J_{2} (M_{F^{(2)}},S^{3n+2k+2}).
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\noindent Considering the homotopy pushout of $\nabla (\bar{j}_{2.5}\vee \mathrm{id})$ and $u_{1}$, we see that the resulting space is 
the homotopy cofiber of $\nabla (\bar{j}_{2.5}\vee \mathrm{id})[a_{1},a_{2}]$ via employing the homotopy pushout of the map $[a_{1},a_{2}]$ and   $S^{n+1}\wedge S^{3n+2k+1} \rightarrow* $.  (Recall that, in a commutative $3\times 2$ diagram of spaces, if the two inner squares are homotopy pushouts, then the outer rectangle is also a homotopy pushout.)
By checking the homology, we deduce that
this resulting space is the 3-cell skeleton of the space $J_{2} (M_{F^{(2)}},S^{3n+2k+2})$ up to homotopy. 
 Then, the  attaching map $S^{4n+2k+2}\rightarrow J_{2} (M_{F^{(2)}}, S^{3n+2k+2})$ of the 3-cell skeleton of the space $J_{2} (M_{F^{(2)}},S^{3n+2k+2})$ can be taken as $$\nabla(\bar{j}_{2.5}\vee \mathrm{id})[a_{1},a_{2}]=[\nabla(\bar{j}_{2.5}\vee \mathrm{id})a_{1},\nabla(\bar{j}_{2.5}\vee \mathrm{id})a_{2}]=[\,\bar{j}_{2.5},\,i].$$
Restoring the original maps,
  we see that $\gamma$ can be taken as $$\gamma=[j_{2.5},\beta] \equiv[j_{2.5},j_{3}j_{4}\circ\Sigma^{2n+k+2}f]\;\mathrm{mod}\,[j_{2.5},I\circ\Sigma^{2n+k+2}f].$$
\noindent Clearly,   $j_{2.5}=j_{3}j_{3.5}$ up to a unit in $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$. Hence, up to a unit in $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$, the map $[j_{2.5},j_{3}j_{4}\circ\Sigma^{2n+k+2}f]$ is equal to
\begin{align}
[j_{3}j_{3.5},j_{3}j_{4}\circ\Sigma^{2n+k+2}f] &= j_{3}\circ [j_{3.5},\;j_{4}\circ\Sigma^{2n+k+2}f] \notag \\
 &= j_{3}\circ [j_{3.5}\circ \Sigma\mathrm{id}_{S^{n}},\,j_{4}\circ\Sigma(\Sigma^{2n+k+1}f)] \notag \\
 &= j_{3}\circ [j_{3.5},\,j_{4}]\circ \Sigma(\mathrm{id}_{S^{n}}\wedge\Sigma^{2n+k+1}f)) \notag \\
 &= j_{3}\circ [j_{3.5},\,j_{4}]\circ (\pm\Sigma^{3n+k+2}f ).\notag 
\end{align} \noindent
 (Here, we freely use the well-known formula of Whitehead products given in \cite[Theorem 8.18, p.~484]{GW}.)
Without changing the homotopy type,  we can choose  $\gamma$ satisfying
$\gamma \equiv j_{3}\circ[j_{3.5},\,j_{4}]\circ\Sigma^{3n+k+2}f\;\mathrm{mod}\,[j_{3}j_{3.5},\;I\circ\Sigma^{2n+k+2}f].$
