label: jssq
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{jssq}  We aim to determine $\pi_{\bullet} (C_{g})=\pi_{\bullet} (Y\cup _{g}CX)$, where $g\colon X\rightarrow Y$ is a map between simply-connected spaces.  There is a cofiber sequence $$ X\xrightarrow[]{g}Y\stackrel{j_{_{Y}}}\hookrightarrow C_{g}\stackrel{q}\twoheadrightarrow \Sigma X. $$\noindent
 The homotopy fiber of the map $q$ is Gray's relative James construction, i.e., $F_{q}=J(M_{Y},X)$. Then we have a fiber sequence $F_{q}\stackrel{i}\rightarrow C_{g}\stackrel{q}\rightarrow \Sigma X$, resulting in an exact sequence of  homotopy groups,
$$\pi_{\bullet+1} (\Sigma X)\stackrel{\partial}\rightarrow \pi_{\bullet} (F_{q})\stackrel{i_{*}\;}\rightarrow\pi_{\bullet} (C_{g})\stackrel{q_{*}}\rightarrow\pi_{\bullet} (\Sigma X)\stackrel{\partial}\rightarrow\pi_{\bullet-1} (F_{q}).$$

\noindent After calculating the $\partial$-images, we have a short exact sequence, $$0\rightarrow \mathrm{Im} (i_{*})\stackrel{\subseteq\;}\rightarrow\pi_{\bullet} (C_{g})\stackrel{q_{*}}\rightarrow\mathrm{Ker} (\partial)\rightarrow0, $$
in which $\mathrm{Im} (i_{*})\cong\mathrm{Coker}(\partial\colon\pi_{\bullet+1} (\Sigma X)\rightarrow \pi_{\bullet} (F_{q}))$. So, the problem is reduced to calculating the $\partial$-images, and solving the group extension problem arising from   generators of $\mathrm{Ker}(\partial)$. \begin{itemize}
    \item [\rm (1)] To calculate the $\partial$-images, we use these formulas:   $$\partial(\Sigma \mathbbm{x})=i_{_{Y}}\circ g\circ \mathbbm{x}, \;\;\partial( \mathbbm{x}\circ\Sigma\mathbbm{y})=\partial( \mathbbm{x})\circ \mathbbm{y},$$  $$\partial\{  \mathbbm{x}_{1}, \Sigma^{k+1}\mathbbm{x}_{2},\Sigma^{k+1}\mathbbm{x}_{3}\} _{k+1}\subseteq (-1)^{k+1} \{  \partial\mathbbm{x}_{1}, \Sigma^{k}\mathbbm{x}_{2},\Sigma^{k}\mathbbm{x}_{3}\} _{k},$$

\noindent
whenever the maps can be composed and the  Toda bracket on the left is well-defined. Here, $$i_{_{Y}}\colon Y\hookrightarrow M_{Y}\hookrightarrow J(M_{Y}, X)=F_{q}$$ \noindent denotes the canonical inclusion. Additionally, $j_{_{Y}}=i\circ i_{_{Y}}$.
\\\indent\quad During this process, we need to rewrite elements as linear combinations of Toda's generators, using the relations given in Toda's book \cite{Toda}, or using $\hat{O}$guchi's table \cite[pp.~103--105]{Og} which is more convenient. 






 \item [\rm (2)]To solve the group extension problem coming from the generators of $\mathrm{Ker}(\partial)$, we use  the following fact. Suppose that $\Sigma\mathbbm{x}\in \mathrm{Ker}(\partial)$ is a generator  of order $m<\infty$  satisfying $g\circ \mathbbm{x}=0$. (In concrete calculations, such an element $\Sigma \mathbbm{x}$ often exists.) Then,  there exists  $$\mathrm{coext}_{g} (\mathbbm{x})\in \mathrm{Coext}_{g} (\mathbbm{x})\subseteq \{  j_{_{Y}},\;g,\;\mathbbm{x} \} \; $$\noindent such that $q_{*} (\mathrm{coext}_{g} (\mathbbm{x}))=-\Sigma\mathbbm{x}$,   
 and hence $$-m (\mathrm{coext}_{g} (\mathbbm{x}))\in j_{_{Y}}\circ\{  g,\;\mathbbm{x},\; [m]\} ,\;\;\big([m]=m(\mathrm{id})\big).
 $$
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 \noindent It remains to analyze the  Toda bracket $\{  g,\;\mathbbm{x}, \;[m]\} $, employing the fundamental properties of Toda brackets given in Toda's book \cite[Proposition 1.2, Proposition 1.4]{Toda}.
\end{itemize}

\label{v42}  Without taking any localization,  the Stiefel manifold
$ V_{2} (\mathbb{C}^{4})=\textit{SU} (4)/\textit{SU} (2)$ has a CW decomposition $V_{2} (\mathbb{C}^{4})\simeq(\Sigma^{3}\mathbb{C}P^{2})\cup e^{12}$ by checking the Steenrod square $\emph{S}q^{2}$ \cite[6.10 (4), p.~624]{mtbook}. Note that there is a  well-known algebra isomorphism   $$H^{*} ( V_{2} (\mathbb{C}^{4});\mathbb{Z})\cong\Lambda(a,b), \,\;(|a|=5,\; |b|=7),$$ where $\Lambda(a,b)$ is the exterior algebra; see \cite[Proposition 5.11, p.~152]{pxljc}. Take an arbitrary point $x_{0}\in V_{2} (\mathbb{C}^{4})$. We know that $V_{2} (\mathbb{C}^{4})=(V_{2} (\mathbb{C}^{4})\backslash\{  x_{0}\} )\cup \mathrm{int} (D^{12} (x_{0}))$, where $D^{12} (x_{0})\subseteq V_{2} (\mathbb{C}^{4})$ is a small disk containing $x_{0}$ of dimension 12. Then, the fact $\pi_{1} (V_{2} (\mathbb{C}^{4}))=0$ and the Van Kampen theorem imply $\pi_{1} (V_{2} (\mathbb{C}^{4})\backslash\{  x_{0}\} )=0.$ It is well-known that $V_{2} (\mathbb{C}^{4})$ is an orientable manifold. Then, making use of the  classical techniques from Hatcher  \cite[Section 3.3, p.~231]{xh}  as well as \cite[Theorem 3.26 (a), p.~236]{xh} to analyze  the exact sequence$$\cdots \rightarrow H_{i}\big(V_{2} (\mathbb{C}^{4})\backslash\{  x_{0}\} ;\mathbb{Z}\big)\rightarrow H_{i}\big(V_{2} (\mathbb{C}^{4});\mathbb{Z}\big)\rightarrow H_{i}\big((V_{2} (\mathbb{C}^{4}),\;V_{2} (\mathbb{C}^{4})\backslash\{  x_{0}\} );\mathbb{Z}\big)\rightarrow\cdots,$$ 
\noindent we see that 
$V_{2} (\mathbb{C}^{4})\backslash\{  x_{0}\} \simeq \Sigma^{3}\mathbb{C}P^{2}.$
